--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page continues the introduction to Geoffroy Tory’s 1549 edition, detailing the specific contents of the three books and the supplemental alphabets provided at the end of the volume.</meta>

The first book contains an exhortation to organize and regulate the French language by a specific rule for speaking elegantly in good and more wholesome <note>original: "plussain," meaning pure or correct</note> French.

The second treats the invention of Attic <note>Tory's term for classical Roman capital letters</note> letters and their proportional comparison to the natural body and face of the perfect human being, along with several beautiful designs and moralities <note>philosophical or symbolic interpretations</note> concerning these Attic letters.

In the third and final book, all the aforementioned Attic letters are drawn and proportioned according to their alphabetical order, in both height and width, each one individually, teaching their proper form and required Latin and French pronunciation, in both the ancient and modern styles.

At the end are added thirteen different styles of letters: specifically Hebrew, Greek, Latin, and French letters—the latter in four styles, which are *Cadeaulx* <note>large, decorative calligraphic capitals often used in legal documents</note>, the bastard form <note>a common hybrid of formal and cursive gothic scripts</note>, and *tourneure* <note>a rounded script</note>. Following these are Persian, Arabic, African, Turkish, and Tartarian letters, all five of which use the same alphabet style. Afterward come the Chaldean, the Gasses—otherwise called Imperial—and the Bullatic <note>letters resembling those used on papal "bulls" or seals</note>. Then, the Fantastic letters, the Utopian—which might be called "voluntary" <note>likely referring to letters created by whim or imagination</note>—and finally, the Flowered letters. Included also are instructions and the method for making letter-ciphers <note>monograms</note> for gold rings, tapestries, stained glass, paintings, and other things as may seem good and beautiful.

<summary>This page outlines the three-part structure of Tory's treatise—covering language reform, the human proportions of letters, and a technical guide to the alphabet—before listing various exotic and decorative scripts included in the appendix.</summary>
<keywords>French language, Attic letters, human proportions, typography, alphabet styles, calligraphy, monograms, exotic scripts</keywords>

<page-type>preface</page-type>
<sig>ã ij</sig>

# Geoffroy Tory of Bourges, gives and offers humble Greeting to all true & devoted lovers of good letters <note>original: "bonnes lettres," a phrase referring to the humanities, classical literature, and the art of fine writing</note>.

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'L' featuring intricate floral and vine patterns within a square border.</image-desc>

The Poets, the Orators, and the other scholars in letters and sciences, when they have created and compiled some work by their studious diligence and hand, are accustomed to present it to some great lord of the Court or of the Church, exalting him through writings and praises to the notice of other men. This is done to please him, and so that they might always be so welcome in his presence that he seems obligated and bound to give them some substantial gift, some Benefice <note>an ecclesiastical office providing an income</note>, or some Office in recompense for the Labors and Vigils <note>original: "Vigiles," referring to the practice of studying and writing late into the night by candlelight</note> they have put into creating and composing their said works and gifts.

I could easily do the same with this little book, but considering that if I presented it to one person rather than another, there might be some envious hesitation, I have decided that it would be more honorable for me to make a present of it to you all, O devoted lovers of good Letters, without preferring the great to the small: except in so far as one loves Letters more and is more steeped in virtue. In this way, the Prelates and great Lords, who are all excellent in beautiful and good virtues, will have their part, so that you will not lose yours. I am displeased that some have tried to discourage me from making public what I am writing to you in this, our complete work, and that they have tried to make me out to be an ungrateful man for not wanting to teach a thing so very beautiful and good.

<vocab>Geoffroy Tory, Bourges, Poets, Orators, Letters, Sciences, Prelates, Lords</vocab>

He addresses the criticism he faced for choosing to share his specialized knowledge of letterforms and language with the general public.</summary>

...which is against the art of Grammar. Likewise, some letters there are almost lying sideways, and others have their feet turned upwards, which is against natural reason. The nature of letters, which are made on the model of the human body, is to be in their required and upright view, standing up, and in their entirety. 

But if someone were to argue against me that on a piece of gold, silver, copper, or other material, there are letters of which some, in relation to others, are found with their feet sideways or turned upwards, I would reply honestly that this is well done, for one can turn the said piece of gold or other object between one's fingers to see each letter in its proper orientation and position. 

But in paintings, stained glass, tapestries, on walls, and in many other places, one cannot turn the letters without turning the entire place where they are set; therefore, it is necessary that they always be planted and written straight, one after the other. Whoever would wish to write on scrolls should not write lengthwise, but crosswise. <margin>The invention of writing on scrolls.</margin>
It is a great foolishness to wish to do something without discerning the reason for it. The invention of writing on scrolls comes from a long and almost unknown antiquity, but I shall tell it to you nonetheless. It came from the ancient Lacedemonians <note>The ancient name for the Spartans, known for their discipline and military ingenuity.</note>, who in times 
<margin>Two identical rods.</margin>
of war had two rods <note>Known as a <term>scytale</term>, this was one of the earliest cryptographic devices.</note> made precisely of the same length and thickness; they gave one to the prince who went to war, and kept the other until they wished to send him some secret. And when they sent a message to him, they took a piece of parchment or leather, or some other similar thing, long and narrow like a belt, and wrapped it edge to edge around and along the rod which they had kept. Then they wrote upon their parchment along and all around their said rod, in such a way that the greater part of the letters was found either by half, or a third, or just a little bit upon the edges and joins of their said parchment. Then they unrolled it and sent it, completely unrolled, to their prince. As soon as he had received it, he would place it around his own rod, and immediately—by the grace of the identical measurement of the two matching rods—all the letters would meet exactly in their entirety, just as they were when they were first written. They did this among themselves so that if by chance their enemies intercepted their posts or messengers, they would not have been able to make sense of the letters thus written across the parchment. # To the Readers of this present book
## a humble greeting.

IT is commonly said, and truly so, that there is great natural virtue in herbs, in stones, and in words. To provide examples of this would be superfluous, so certain is the truth of it. But I wish it might please God to grant me the grace that I could do so much through my words and requests as to persuade some that, if they do not wish to bring honor to our French language, they should at least not corrupt it. I find that there are three types of men who delight and strive to corrupt and deform it.
<margin>Latin-skimmers.</margin>
These are the Latin-skimmers, the jesters, and the jargoners.
<margin>Jesters.</margin>
When the Latin-skimmers <note>original: "eſcumeurs de Latin." These were scholars or students who used an absurdly Latinized French, a practice famously mocked by Tory’s contemporary, François Rabelais.</note> say, "let us skim the Latian verbocination <note>original: "verbocination latiale," meaning Latinate speech-making.</note>, and trans-ferry the Seine at
<margin>Jargoners.</margin>
dilucule and crepuscule <note>original: "dilucule & crepuſcule," meaning dawn and dusk.</note>, then deambulate through the Crossroads and Squares of Lutetia <note>original: "Lutece," the Roman name for Paris.</note>, and like truth-loving suitors capture the benevolence of the sleep-bringing and all-formed female sex," it seems to me that they do not only mock their peers, but their very own selves.
<margin>Skimmed language.</margin>
When the jesters—whom I can honestly call language-shredders—say, "Mr. Page, if you do not give me a slice of the day <note>original: "leſche du iour," likely slang for a piece of bread or a snack.</note>, I commit myself to God, and I tell you this: you shall have a bloody flick on the nose," they seem to me to do as much damage to our language as they do to their clothes by shredding and wastefully consuming that which is worth
<margin>Shredded language.</margin>
more when whole than when wickedly cut and mutilated. In the very same way, when jargoners hold...

I would cite a little of the aforementioned jargon, but to avoid the wicked knowledge of it, I shall pass over it, and I say that I wish such corruptors of honest language were so prudent and wise that they might consider that a man who wishes to be truly well-versed in pure virtue <term>virtue: For Tory, linguistic purity is a moral obligation; "vertu" implies both excellence of character and the inherent power of the language.</term> ought always and in every place to do and say things that are beautiful, good, and honest. 

Men are known by their deeds and by their words. Let us, therefore, ensure that our sayings and words are healthy and acceptable, in all reason and all honor. Let us accustom ourselves to speak well and to say well; in doing so, we shall find that we will benefit from it, and that our words will have such great virtue that they will persuade through a thousand beautiful expressions. 

O devoted lovers of good letters, would that it please God that some noble heart would employ himself to set and arrange our French language by rule! This would be the means by which many thousands of men would strive to frequently use beautiful and good words. If it is not so established and ordered, it will be found that from one fifty-year period to the next, the 
<margin>
The author of the Book of Chess.
</margin>
French language will, for the most part, be changed and perverted. Today's language is changed in a thousand ways from the language that existed fifty years ago or thereabouts. The author of the Book of Chess <note>Tory likely refers to Jacques de Cessoles, whose moralizing work on chess was a staple of late medieval literature and underwent many linguistic updates.</note>...

<summary>Tory condemns the use of criminal slang (jargon), specifically citing François Villon, and calls for the establishment of formal grammatical rules to stabilize the French language, which he observes changes drastically every fifty years.</summary>
<keywords>jargon, gallows, François Villon, linguistic purity, virtue, standardization of French, Book of Chess, linguistic evolution</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Geoffroy Tory’s argument for the standardization of French. Having just discussed the "jargon" of criminals, he now illustrates how much the common French language has shifted over time, comparing medieval usage to his own era (the early 16th century), and expresses a desire for a definitive French grammar.</meta>

...as each said in his time. Just as we now say, "No more" <note>original: 'Non plus'</note>, whereas they used to say "Naught more" <note>original: 'Neant plus'</note>. He would say: "It is truth" <note>original: 'Bien est voir'</note>, and we say "It is true" <note>original: 'Bien est vray'</note>. In exactly the same way he would say, "Hold straight," "Does not want," and "The vowel," <note>Tory lists archaic pronunciations 'Tenroit', 'Ve volt pas', and 'Le voyeu' against the modern 'Tien droit', 'Ne veult pas', and 'La vocale'.</note> where we say them differently. He said a thousand other things that I omit for brevity. One could find ten thousand of such words and terms abandoned and changed, which a hundred other authors used in times past. In those past times, it was common 
<margin>
Ancient Language.
</margin>
to say "Herper" for "To play the Harp." One said, "To assemble with one’s enemy" for "To begin to fight." "Lance stiff upon the felt" meant "Lance placed upon the rest." And "To sound the hails for the assault" meant "To sound the trumpets." "To be burdened" <note>original: 'affessé'</note> meant to be weighed down. "May it not grieve you" meant "May it not displease you." "To put his sword back in its 'feurre'" meant to put it back in the scabbard. "To mis-advise" <note>original: 'Forconseiller'</note> meant to give bad advice. "To whirlwind" meant to make a great wind. And there are a thousand other similar examples one could give, of which one could make a large and proper volume. I would have cause to lament the sterility of our hands <note>A metaphor for the lack of formal rules or "tools" (grammars) produced by French writers.</note>, but I hope that by the pleasure of God some noble Priscian, some Donatus, or some French Quintilian <note>Priscian, Donatus, and Quintilian were the most famous grammarians and rhetoricians of Roman antiquity; Tory is calling for a French scholar to do for French what they did for Latin.</note> shall be born soon, if he is not already fully formed. I find, furthermore, that there is another class of men who corrupt our language even more grievously. These are the Innovators and 
<margin>
Forgers of new words.
</margin>
Forgers of new words. If such forgers are not scoundrels, I consider them hardly better. Consider that they think they have a great elegance when they say, after drinking, that they have their brains...

<meta>catchword: ...brains.</meta>

<summary>Tory provides a list of archaic French terms to demonstrate how the language evolves and decays without formal rules, calling for a French grammarian to codify the tongue. He also begins a critique of "innovators" who invent nonsensical new vocabulary.</summary>

--- Page 20 ---
<meta>This page continues Geoffroy Tory’s argument for the standardization of French. Having previously discussed the corruption of the language through regional dialects and "slang," he concludes his introductory plea by urging French scholars to collaborate in refining their mother tongue into a tool as precise and beautiful as Latin or Greek.</meta>

...completely muddled <note>original: 'encornimatibulé'</note>, and obsessed with a heap of wonderful-sounding nonsense <note>original: 'mirilifiques & triquedōdaines'</note>, a pile of trifles and gibberish that incessantly confuse them. I would not have cited such foolish words, had it not been that the disdain of thinking about it compelled me to do so. 
<margin>Juvenal</margin>
*If nature denies it, indignation makes the verse.* <note>A famous line from the Roman satirist Juvenal (Satire 1.79), suggesting that even if one lacks natural poetic talent, anger at the state of the world can provide the inspiration to write.</note>
Indignation has constrained me to show this foolishness. I believe there is no way to purely organize such language, for the characters who forge it are incapable of sound reason. Nonetheless, if our language were duly regulated and polished, such filth could be cast out from it. Therefore, I pray you, let us all give courage to one another, and let us awaken to purify it. All things have had a beginning. When one treats the letters, and another the vowels, a third will come who will define the dictions <note>proper word choices or vocabulary</note>, and then yet another will emerge who will organize beautiful oratory. By such means, we will find that little by little we will make our way, until we arrive at the great fields of poetry and rhetoric, full of beautiful, good, and fragrant flowers of speech, to speak properly and easily everything that one might wish.

->Wholly yours, Geoffroy Tory of Bourges.<-

<summary>Geoffroy Tory concludes his preface by calling on French scholars to systematically reform the language, moving from basic letters to complex rhetoric. He envisions a future where French is as "flowery" and expressive as the classical languages.</summary>
<keywords>Geoffroy Tory, Juvenal, poetry, rhetoric, linguistics, French language reform, Champ Fleury</keywords>

# The Art & Science of the
## Due & True Proportion of <term>Attic letters</term><note>Tory uses "Attic" (referring to Athens/Greece) to signify classical, elegant proportions, which he equates here with "Ancient" or "Roman" typography.</note>, which are otherwise called ancient letters & commonly Roman letters.

<margin>
Jean Grolier, lover of good letters and beloved by them.
</margin>
<margin>
Cicero
</margin>
<image-desc>A large ornamental drop cap 'L' decorated with intricate white vine and floral scrollwork on a dark hatched background, enclosed in a square frame.</image-desc>On the morning of the day of the <note>original: "feste aux Roys." The Feast of Kings, or Epiphany, celebrated on January 6th.</note> Feast of Kings, after having taken my sleep and rest, and when my stomach had easily digested its light and joyful meal, in the year 1523, I began to muse in my bed and turn the wheel of my memory, thinking of a thousand small fancies, as much serious as joyful. Among these, I remembered some Ancient letters that I had recently designed for the house of my lord the treasurer of wars, Master <note>Jean Grolier (1479–1565) was one of history’s most famous book collectors and a high-ranking French official. He was known for his motto "Io. Grolierii et amicorum" (For Jean Grolier and his friends).</note> Jean Grolier, Counselor and Secretary to our lord the King, a lover of good letters and of all learned personages, by whom he is also greatly loved and esteemed both across and on this side of the mountains <note>A common Renaissance phrase referring to Italy (across the Alps) and France (this side of the Alps).</note>. And in thinking of those Attic letters, there suddenly came to my memory a sententious passage from the first book and eighth chapter of <note>A foundational work of moral philosophy by the Roman statesman Cicero.</note> Cicero’s *Offices*, where it is written: <note>original Latin: "Nõ nobis solùm nati sumus, ortúsque nostri, partem patria."</note> *We are not born for ourselves alone, and of our birth, a part [is owed to] our country...*

<summary>In this opening passage, Geoffroy Tory describes the moment of inspiration for his treatise, which occurred on Epiphany in 1523 while reflecting on letterforms he designed for the famous bibliophile Jean Grolier. He invokes Cicero to justify his work as a contribution to the public good and his country.</summary>
<keywords>Geoffroy Tory, Jean Grolier, Cicero, Attic letters, Roman letters, typography, Epiphany, 1523, De Officiis</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the sentence from the previous page, completing a famous Latin quote from Cicero’s "De Officiis." Tory is moving from his personal recollections to a formal declaration of his intent: to standardize the French language and its typography for the "public good."</meta>

# On the Proportion of Letters

...claims a share, and our friends another. <note>original: "vendicat, partem amici." This concludes the quote from Cicero mentioned on the previous page: "Non nobis solum nati sumus, ortusque nostri partem patria vindicat, partem amici" (We are not born for ourselves alone; our country claims a share of our birth, and our friends another).</note> Which is to say, in substance, that we are not born into this world only to be of service and pleasure to our friends and our country. For this reason, wishing to employ myself in some way for the utility of the <term>public good</term><note>A Renaissance ideal (pro bono publico) where scholars felt a duty to share knowledge for the benefit of society rather than keeping it for an elite few.</note>, I have thought to demonstrate and teach in this present small work the manner of making letters symmetrically. That is to say, by due proportion, the <term>Attic letter</term>, of which I see many men on this side of the mountains <note>Meaning within France (on the French side of the Alps).</note> who wish to use it, but are poorly skilled, insofar as they do not know what measure and proportion it ought to have. I would also treat the <term>Letter of Form</term> and the <term>Bastarda</term><note>"Letter of Form" (lettre de Forme) refers to the heavy, formal Gothic blackletter script used for Bibles and liturgical books. "Bastarda" (Bastarde) was a more informal, cursive Gothic script used for legal and everyday documents.</note>; but for this time, our Lord helping, I will design the said Attic letter alone. Some have wished to dissuade me from doing this, saying that I should not make it so manifest, but keep it secret for myself. Saving their honor, it seems to me not so, and that I should not be a glutton for honest and good knowledge. I would have treated and written of it in Latin, as I could well do, I believe, and as one can recognize from the small Latin works that I have had printed and placed before the eyes of good students, as much in meter as in prose. But wishing to somewhat decorate our <term>French language</term>, and so that, along with people of good letters, the common people might use it, I wish to write of it in French. I am sure that soon some detractor and envious person will arise who will say that I wish to act as a "New Author," and will force himself to bite at my institutions and teachings. But I know, according to the ancient Poets and Philosophers,
<margin>Momus.</margin> that <term>Momus</term><note>In Greek mythology, Momus was the god of satire and mockery, often used by Renaissance authors to represent those who criticize the work of others without creating anything themselves.</note> was a rogue who never knew...

<summary>Geoffroy Tory explains his decision to write his treatise in French rather than Latin to benefit the public and "decorate" the language, focusing on the correct proportions of Roman (Attic) letters.</summary>
<keywords>Geoffroy Tory, typography, French language, Cicero, public good, Attic letters, Gothic script, Momus, Renaissance education</keywords>

<meta>This page continues from the author’s justification for his work. He is addressing potential critics by invoking the mythological figure of Momus, the personification of mockery, before explaining his methodology based on geometric principles.</meta>

### Book One.

<margin>The sandal & fabric of Venus.</margin>
...nothing to do but mock, as when he mocked the Sandal and Fabric of Venus, saying that there were too many glittering and clinking spangles, and that it made too much noise. <margin>Nature.</margin> Similarly, he mocked Mother Nature because she had <margin>Neptune.</margin> placed horns upon the foreheads of bulls and cows rather than on <margin>Minerva</margin> their shoulders, so as to strike more impetuously. He <margin>& their masterpiece.</margin> also mocked the bull of Neptune, the house of Minerva, and the man of Vulcan. But especially he mocked this man, because the <margin>The man of Vulcan.</margin> said Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire and metalworking, known for his craftsmanship.</note> had not made any window or shutter in his chest, so that through them one might know what he was thinking and pondering in his said chest, which is full of hollow and winding places. ## On the Proportion of Letters

That he is depicted as an old man is nothing to wonder at; for indeed, eloquence alone is accustomed to show its full vigor only in old age. If only what your poets say is true: "A dense mist covers the hearts of the young." <note>This refers to the idea that youth is clouded by passion or ignorance, whereas age brings clarity.</note> Conversely, old age is able to speak something better and more noble than raw youth. Furthermore, as for this old Hercules drawing people bound by their ears to his tongue—he who is none other than Speech itself—you should not wonder at this either, since you are not ignorant of the kinship <margin>The kinship of the tongue with the ears.</margin> between the tongue and the ears. Nor does it pertain to his insult that his tongue is pierced. For I remember, he said, some iambic verses from your comedies saying that the very tip of the tongue is perforated in all talkative men. In short, we hold this opinion of him: that whatever he did, he accomplished through speech and eloquence. <margin>Hercules as a wise man.</margin> As a wise man, he subdued most things to himself through persuasion. Indeed, his arrows are surely sharp, far-reaching, and swift arguments that wound the soul, which is why they are called "winged" <note>original: *pannigera*. This literally means "clothed in rags" or "winged," referring to the feathers on an arrow, but used here metaphorically for sharp-witted speech.</note>. Thus far the Gaul.

# Book One. THE GALLIC HERCULES <note>original: "HERCVLES GALLICVS"</note>.

[Image: A woodcut showing Hercules as an old man representing Eloquence. Chains of gold and silver extend from his tongue to the ears of his followers, symbolizing how the French are led by persuasive speech rather than brute force.]

### THE FRENCH HERCULES.

If there were a certain rule to accompany our eloquence <term>facundité: fluency or rhetorical skill</term>, it seems to me, subject to correction, that our language would be richer and more perfect. And in this regard—because I remember it, and so that I may provide some good reason why a rule could be established here, since I commonly see many people, both learned and unlearned, fail and commit barbarisms <note>Errors in usage or pronunciation</note> and inept language—I say that for the perfect preterits <term>preteritz parfaictz: the simple past tense (e.g., "he did" vs. "he has done")</term> one can assign such a rule, and say:

<margin>Note here the rule of Grammar in French.</margin>
Every time that the infinitive ends in *re*, the preterit in the third person singular must be pronounced in *it*: as in *batre* [to hit], which becomes *batit* [he hit]; *faire* [to do/make], which becomes *feit* [he did]; and *vaincre* [to defeat], which becomes *vainquit* [he defeated]. *Plaire* [to please] and its compounds, which are *complaire* [to comply] and *deſplaire* [to displease], are exceptions to this: for they make their preterit in *eut*: *pleut* [it pleased], *compleut*, and *deſpleut*. *Boyre* [to drink] also, and *croire* [to believe], become *beut* and *creut*. Similarly, *Eſtre* [to be] makes its said preterit...

He argues that formal rules will make the French language as "perfect" and "rich" as the classical tongues.</summary>

<margin>In Greek there are five different dialects governed by rules: Johannes Grammaticus.</margin>

<margin>Abraham. Moses.</margin>
Abraham, the ancient philosopher and the prince of sovereign Patriarchs, according to the opinion of some, was the first inventor of letters. Moses, according to other opinions, first gave the knowledge of them to the Jews. From these Jews, the Phoenicians gained notice of them, and then the Greeks from the said Phoenicians.

Cadmus <note>In Greek mythology, the Phoenician prince who founded Thebes and brought the alphabet to the Greeks.</note>, according to Cornelius Tacitus, and according to Pliny in the aforementioned chapter and book, gave them to the said Greeks. > Tyre, if one is pleased to believe rumor, either first taught or first learned letters.
<note>original Latin: *Tyrus, si famæ libet credere, literas prima aut docuit, aut didicit.*</note>

They wanted their victories and arrogance to be memorialized by their Latin letters, thinking to surpass the Greek language—a thing they could not do, as the Greek language is composed of better-ordered letters, such that it is beyond comparison more fertile, abundant, and flourishing than their Latin.

# Of the Proportion of Letters

...watch and write for the utility of the public good, and the exaltation of perfect Knowledge.

<margin>I and O are the model for all the other Attic letters</margin>
**I** return then to our aforementioned Attic letters <note>Tory refers to Roman capital letters as "Attic" letters, associating them with the elegance of ancient Greek culture</note>, and say regarding the aforementioned fable of Io, that these two letters here, .I, and O, are the two letters from which all the others are made and formed. The A is made only of the I. The B is made of the said I, and of a broken O <note>meaning a curved stroke or "bowl"</note>. The C is made only of a broken O. The D, of an I and a broken O. And similarly all the others are made of one of the said two letters, or of both together, as I shall say hereafter, and shall show by figure and symmetry, our Lord helping. One can also say that the O is made from the I <note>likely referring to rotating the I or using it as a radius</note>, but we can consider that the O is the model for the bowls <note>original: "panses"</note> and roundings of letters other than itself.

<margin>Well worth noting.</margin>
**N**ote in passing that Io, for the name of the beautiful daughter of Inachus, should be written with Iota and Omega <note>original: "I$\Omega$"</note>. That is to say, with an I, as a vowel, and by an Omega, which is long in metrical syllable quantity. But for my purpose, IO shall be written with Omicron. That is to say, with an O, short in syllable quantity, because it is a simple and uniform letter, and because it is more suitable for making a good demonstration for proportioning the roundnesses of the other letters than is the said Omega. This Omega is also made from the said Omicron by writing it twice, joined to one another, according to the reason and rule of Grammar, which requires that a vowel long in metrical quantity be worth two shorts, and two shorts worth one long.

# Book One.

# On the Proportion of Letters

...aspiration H. But in ancient times, the shape of the said aspiration was not written at all. However, the Greeks, since the aforementioned fiction and fable was created, have put it into use in their regular language over their seven vowels, which are: **A, E, H, I, O, Y, Ω** <note>Alpha, Epsilon, Eta, Iota, Omicron, Upsilon, and Omega</note>. And they used it over a single consonant named **Rho** <note>The letter 'P', often aspirated in Greek as 'Rh'</note>. They used these not as letters, but as accents, and they wrote them only above the said vowels and consonant, outside the line of the letters. The Latins have utilized it differently than the said Greeks and have written it on the line, mixing it among several of their letters, so much so that it is almost regarded as a true letter.

<margin>Of the A, a triangular letter.</margin>
I have said that the letter **A**, which is the first of the alphabet—otherwise called the **A, B, C**—is made from the letter **I**, and this is true, by shaping it into a triangle, which is an odd number. The two legs of the said **A** and the head form the said triangle, but this triangle must be seated within a square, which is signified to us by the word **Hyacinthus**, which contains four syllables: **Hy, a, cin, thus**.

<margin>Attic letters are all made of three geometric figures: Round, Square, and Triangular. Virgil.</margin>
The ancients, wishing to show the singular perfection of their letters, formed and shaped them by the due proportion of the three best and most perfect figures of Geometry, which are: the **Round** figure, the **Square**, and the **Triangular**. And because odd numbers have always been considered lucky among the Ancients, and they held them in such great reverence that they were even included in ceremonies and sacrifices—as we still see in our churches with the glorious **Trinity**, and that in the singing of High Mass there is a **Priest**, **Deacon**, and **Subdeacon**—and as **Virgil** said in his eighth Eclogue: *In number...* <note>original Latin: "Numero deus impare gaudet" — God delights in an odd number.</note>

<meta>catchword: In number</meta>

# Book One.

*God delights in an odd number.* <note>original: "Deus impare gaudet," a quote from Virgil's Eclogues 8.75</note> That is to say, God loves the odd number. They have made their first letter an odd number <note>The letter 'A', being the first letter and triangular, representing the number 3</note> seated upon the square of an even number <note>The number 4</note> to provide a good beginning and happy access to those who will love and wish to study the liberal arts <note>original: "les bonnes lettres," referring to the humanities and classical literature</note>.

<margin>Macrobius on the even and odd number</margin>
The odd number, as Macrobius says in the first book of *The Saturnalia* <note>A 5th-century Latin work that was highly influential in the Renaissance for its encyclopedic knowledge and Neoplatonic philosophy</note>, is taken for the male, and the even number for the female. This is to say that by the conjunction of male and female, man is engendered. Likewise, by the conjunction of letters, syllables are made, and by the conjunction of syllables, words. And Speech <note>original: "l’Oraison," here meaning formal discourse or prose</note>, through the gathering of letters, syllables, and words well-harmonized, is found to be good, elegant, and smooth-flowing.

THE aforementioned Triangle and Square are also contained within a circle, which is the figure containing more than any other figure. This denotes that the perfect and ample knowledge of the Muses and the noble sciences resides and lies within the liberal arts, through which one can read and study, write and assemble in books and memory—as the good Philosophers and ancient authors did in the past, and as we are able to do by exercising ourselves day and night in reading and writing the aforementioned liberal arts and sciences.

## On the Proportion of Letters

> *“A pipe, which Dametas once gave me as a gift.”* <note>original Latin: "Fistula, Damætas dono mihi quem dedit olim." From Virgil's second Eclogue.</note>

<margin>The moral meaning of Virgil’s flute.</margin>
“I have,” said he, “a flute <note>The original French uses *flageol*, a small flute or pipe.</note> that has seven holes in an odd number, which Dametas gave me long ago as a pure gift.” By this flute, which is long and round and turned on a lathe, our two aforementioned letters, I and O, can be understood <note>The straight body of the flute represents the I, while the roundness and the holes represent the O.</note>; and by the seven holes, the seven Liberal Arts that I have illustrated and arranged above. We commonly see that on the back of a flute there are seven holes arranged by measure, one after another; but underneath there is one for the thumb, which represents Apollo <note>The Greek and Roman god of music, poetry, and light, often depicted as the leader of the Muses.</note> alongside the seven Liberal Arts. And furthermore, for greater harmony, we also see on the said flute another hole which is on the side near the back end, which makes the ninth hole, and represents the perfection and fulfillment of the nine Muses together with the seven Liberal Arts. And if, with these nine Muses, you still wish to find Apollo: the hole near the mouth, in which the sound of all the other holes is made and harmonized, shall signify the said Apollo.

<margin>Even and Odd numbers. Virgil.</margin>
Therefore, see how in good literature and the Sciences the good Ancients used even and odd numbers <note>original: "nombre Per & Imper," from the Latin *par* (even) and *impar* (odd).</note>, just as the said Virgil did in the first book of his *Aeneid* when he said:

> *“O three and four times blessed.”* <note>original Latin: "O térque quatérque beati."</note>

They used them, I say—the good Ancients—by secretly understanding them to mean the seven Liberal Arts and the nine Muses with their Apollo. I have hereafter drawn the said flute of Virgil, to better place before your eyes the truth of my words and reasoning.

# Of the Proportion of Letters

[heigh]t and width of them according to their form. By Prudence, rule and compass. By Fortitude <note>original: "Force"</note>, continual and stubborn perseverance to divide, measure, and duly proportion them. By Temperance <note>original: "Atrempence"</note>, a certain discretion to set them between two principal equidistant lines, and to lodge them there in due space, near or far from one another, according to what is appropriate for them.

<margin>A regular note.</margin>
Consider in the said figure, divided into four parts, how the human face matches the division, and the division matches it. The pupil of the eye, set upon the centric and diametrical line, shows us what I have said above: that every letter having a joint <term>joint</term> <note>original: "briseure." In typography, this refers to the point where strokes meet or intersect, such as the crossbar of an A or the middle of an E.</note> must have it set precisely upon the said centric line, and nowhere else.

Upon this face, between the two eyes, all along the nose, and above the mouth, we shall designate our proportionary and triumphal letter I, to always better explain our reasons, which have already been written several times above.

<margin>Arrangement of the length and width of the I, upon the human face.</margin>
Fine minds can perceive in this place the divine contemplation of the Ancients, who wished to shape their long proportionary letter from the highest line of the square to the lowest, and from the top of the human face to the bottom of the chin; they imagined it between the two eyes, taking due proportion there, just as the nose in a well-formed man is the measure of his entire body by dimensions made in numbers multiplied by a certain ratio. # Second Book.

...of the twenty-four letters, as well as the nine Muses, the seven Liberal Arts, the four Cardinal Virtues, and the three Graces, has been secretly fashioned, constituted, and matched to the number of vital channels and the most noble members of the human body, which are likewise twenty-three in number.

<margin>A notable and beautiful comparison.</margin>
Firstly, for the nine Muses and the nine Mutes <note>In the phonetics of this era, "mutes" were letters pronounced without an accompanying vowel sound, such as B, C, D, G, P, T, K, Q.</note>, we shall take the nine channels of the vital spirit, of which, as I have written above, seven are in the head and the other two are below the belly. Those of the head are the two ears, the two eyes, the two nostrils, and the mouth. The other two are the natural member for urinating and the place behind for discharging the belly.

<margin>Profound speculation and agreement.</margin>
For the seven Liberal Arts <note>The traditional curriculum of Grammar, Logic, Rhetoric, Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, and Astronomy.</note> and the seven Semivowels <note>Letters that have a sound of their own but require a vowel to be fully voiced, usually F, L, M, N, R, S, X.</note>, we shall take the brain, the lungs, the liver, the heart, the spleen, the navel, and the pubic region. For the four Cardinal Virtues <note>Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance.</note> and the three Graces, likewise for the five Latin vowels, for the Ypsilon <note>The letter Y.</note>, and for the aspiration H, we shall take the two hands, the two feet, the two shoulders, and the tailbone <note>original: "cropion."</note>. In this way, we shall harmoniously find that the human body and the perfect man are the model and rule for the number of the letters, as well as for the nine Muses, the seven Liberal Arts, the four Cardinal Virtues, and the three Graces—all of which have now been recounted several times to good purpose. To better confirm this in truth and to make its reasoning more apparent, I have portrayed and drawn below two figures of a man: one for the lodging of the letters, and the other for the said Muses and their followers.

## Second Book.

...around, and the third even more shortened: just so among our Attic letters <note>Tory uses "Attic letters" to refer to Roman capitals, reflecting the Renaissance belief in the Greek origins of Roman letterforms.</note> there are those seen in full surface and squareness. That is to say, they are as wide as they are high. Others are less wide, and others still narrower in their width; this is what I have already stated before, when I wrote how many "bodies" <note>In Tory's system, a "body" is a specific unit of measurement derived from the thickness of the letter "I".</note> wide each of our said letters should be. The height in each and every case, except for the Q, must always be equal between two equidistant parallel lines containing a space of ten bodies between them—that is, ten times the thickness of the I. Furthermore, the letter Q has its head of ten bodies like the other letters, but its tail is four bodies long, which extends beyond the aforementioned ten bodies, outside and below the said two equidistant lines.

<margin>
Arrangement and agreement of Faces and letters in perspective.
</margin>
The present figure teaches us how, just as a man’s face, while keeping its height, can sometimes be as wide as it is high—specifically when viewed from the front—and at other times less wide, depending on how it is turned. All our letters, as I have said before, always aim to be of a uniform height, but not of a uniform width; and the reason for this again follows the nature of the human body, and likewise of the face.

<margin>
A singular and general noteworthy point.
</margin>
We see that there are men larger in body and face than others, and some more nimble, more dexterous, and more agile. Some are healthier, and others wiser. Some are more virtuous, and others less so; so too are there letters that are more noble and more worthy than others.

## Book Second.

An example in French will only be when it is placed in a syllable and not as a word <term>diction: Tory’s term for a standalone word or meaningful unit of speech</term>; for "I" cannot be, nor make, a word in our language, although in ciphers and counting it is often used for one <note>Referring to the Roman numeral "I".</note>. Similarly, "O" can form both a syllable and a word. As a syllable: *swan*, *omen* <note>original Latin: "olor" and "omen".</note>. <margin>V. 
Manageable 
Letters.</margin> 
The "V" <note>In the 16th century, 'U' and 'V' were often used interchangeably; here Tory treats it as a vowel.</note> is only used in a syllable, for in Latin it does not form a word by itself. The Picard <note>The dialect of the Picardy region in northern France.</note> does indeed use the said "V" as a word when he says: *He is our son*, or *He is my husband* <note>original Picard: "V, eſt no fieux, V, eſt men baron." <margin>Liquid 
Letters. 
L. M. 
N. R.</margin> 
There are other letters that are "manageable" <note>maniables: flexible or malleable in their pronunciation.</note> and so easy in their power that they flow, and almost as if invisible, they vanish in some syllables when they follow a Mute <term>Mute: a consonant like P, B, T, or D that involves a full stop of breath.</term>. They do not always assist the length of the vowels placed before them, and these are called in Latin: *Liquids, because they melt when placed after Mutes in the same syllable* <note>original Latin: "liquidæ, quia liquefecunt poſt Mutas poſitæ in eadem ſyllaba."</note>. The Liquids, which are four in number—namely L, M, N, R—are so fluid in metrical quantity that they sometimes create a "position"—that is, they make the preceding vowel long—and sometimes they leave it short, as in these Latin words: *Of the father*, *Darkness*, *Pools* <note>original Latin: "Patris", "Tenebræ", "Stagna".</note>. This can be seen more fully in Terentianus <note>Terentianus Maurus, a 2nd-century grammarian who wrote a famous treatise on letters and syllables in verse.</note> where he says:

<margin>Terentian</margin> 
> *Behold, the pools are wet; thus, by a triple pact,* 
> *the syllable is not only rendered long by the addition of time,* 
> *but it also gives strength to the twin powers to increase the Trochee.* <note>original Latin: "Ecce ſtagna madent, triplici ſic ſyllaba pacto / Temporis acceſſu non tantum eſt reddita longa, / ſed dedit & viris geminis augere Trochæum." This explains how a syllable containing a liquid can vary in its "weight" or length in poetry.</note>

# Second Book

<margin>A beautiful fable.</margin>

<margin>The golden chain of the noble Greek Poet Homer.</margin>
Whoever wishes, he says, to speculate and contemplate well, will find a chain and connection that maintains itself through interlocking links and hangs from heaven down to earth. This is to say that every spiritual and physical infusion that we can have here below comes and proceeds from the sovereign Creator of the whole world. Let us therefore imagine here, and think that we see this aforementioned golden chain hanging from heaven down to our feet, and that this chain is of a length and width well-proportioned and suitable to the symmetry of our proportional letter **I**. Thus we shall recognize that Homer’s fiction has understanding regarding the inspiration and invention of good letters and sciences, which could not—and cannot—be known without divine help and inspiration.

...to show that they understand something of the matter, more by pretense than by true knowledge or experience; therefore, I leave them to their opinion, which is poorly founded in reason.

Few people would have thought that our aforementioned King of the Greek Poets, **Homer**, through his **golden chain**, had secretly—and under the shell of a poetic fable—meant the divine inspiration of letters and Sciences, and the connection between them. However, upon looking very closely, he did indeed; although at first glance, it seems not to be so. To give the devoted lovers of good literature something to ponder and consider, I will cite it here so that it may be clearly seen and understood.

# Of the Proportion of Letters

"...how much I excel both the Gods and humans." <note>original Latin: "quantum ego Deos simul atque homines antecello."</note> This is to say in English, just as **Jupiter** is introduced speaking, when he says:

<margin>The Homeric golden chain.</margin>
If you wish to test my virtues and strength, and want certain instruction from me, hurry and hang a golden chain from heaven; and if all of you, as many Gods as Goddesses, are able, pull me from here down to earth: I know that with all your power you will not be able to do it. But when I am angered, if it pleases me, I will pull you all up and scatter you here and there across the land and sea. And there is even more: with this aforementioned golden chain, I could lift the universal earth and the sea to the very heights of the Olympic heaven. And by this, understand how much I exceed and surpass the Gods in power, and likewise human beings.

<margin>Moral sense.</margin>
Therefore, it is quite fitting that this aforementioned golden chain, which we have applied to our **I**, shall signify to us in a moral sense how the knowledge and inspiration of letters comes to us from heaven and from God; that these letters are so kindred and closely connected that they all participate in one another, and similarly the sciences, and consequently the Virtues.

<margin>Virgil imagined a golden bough in a moral sense.</margin>
**Virgil**, the great imitator of **Homer**, in place of this aforementioned golden chain, imagined and fashioned a **golden bough** for his **Aeneas**, which is to say in a moral sense that every man of letters and virtue carries in his hand—that is to say, for his use—a bough of **Wisdom** <term>Sapience: from the Latin 'sapientia,' referring to deep spiritual or philosophical wisdom</term>, which is of gold, as it is the most precious of all metals. The **Sibyl** <note>In the Aeneid, the Sibyl of Cumae guides Aeneas through the underworld.</note>—that is, divine inspiration—says to **Aeneas**—that is, to the devoted lover and...

Because the aspiration is not entirely considered a true letter, it is written on the lowest leaf.

Book Second.

...the said 24 links to the 24 letters that I have written inside the rays of the Sun, each one placed apart, one after the other, aligned with each link, and on the outside between the said rays of the Sun. I have also written and positioned the nine Muses, the seven liberal arts, the four cardinal virtues, and the three Graces, each placed apart from the others; and right in the middle of the 'O', I have designed and portrayed Apollo playing his divine harp.

<margin>Moral meaning.</margin>
To show that the concatenation <note>A series of interconnected things; a chain.</note> and circular perfection of letters, Muses, liberal arts, cardinal virtues, and Graces are inspired and nurtured in us by Apollo—that is to say, by the Sun, or if you prefer to put it better, say by our true God and Creator who is the true Sun. Without His help, every body and every spirit is always dull and useless, and without Him we can have no knowledge within us of letters, of science, or of any virtue whatsoever.

<margin>Rule of Geometry.</margin>
The roundness of the 'O', in its squaring, and also the roundness of the Homeric golden chain <note>A reference to the "Golden Chain" in Homer's Iliad, which Renaissance thinkers often interpreted as a symbol of the divine link between the Creator and the physical world.</note> applied to the said 'O', signifies to us the perfection and adherence of all virtues that every good student should possess. It is a certainty in geometry that a round figure, whether solid or not, is the most capable and the most perfect of all.

# On the Proportion of Letters

...of two lines, from which all our <term>Attic letters</term> <note>Tory uses "Attic" to refer to the elegant Roman or classical letterforms he advocates for, contrasting them with Gothic or "barbaric" styles.</note> are formed. These are the perpendicular line and the balanced horizontal line, making a right and equal angle in a square, about which I have written in several passages in the second book.

<margin>The Ephesians used the Cross in the magical arts</margin>
Furthermore, when the Ephesians wanted to use their magic letters—which they wrote on certain parts of their bodies to obtain victories and to successfully conclude their business, as Erasmus testifies in his second <term>Chiliad</term> <note>original: "Chiliade." A reference to Erasmus's 'Adagia', a massive collection of Greek and Latin proverbs organized into groups of one thousand (Chiliades).</note> at the 79th Proverb, titled *Ephesian letters* <note>original: "Ephesiæ literæ." These were ancient Greek mystical formulas or "charms" thought to protect the wearer.</note>—they made the sign of the Cross there, thinking they would more quickly obtain what they intended.

<margin>The World is marked with a Cross.</margin>
They used the Cross because they saw that the World is marked with a Cross. That is to say, in the East, the West, the South, and the North.

<margin>Man is a little World.</margin>
And also that man—who is, as some Philosophers say, and as is clearly demonstrated in the 30th Chapter of the book on the game of Chess <note>Likely referring to the 'Liber de moribus hominum et officiis nobilium ac popularium super ludo scaccorum' by Jacobus de Cessolis, which used chess to explain human society and morality.</note>—is a <term>Microcosm</term> <note>original: "Mικρóκoσμoς" (Mikrokosmos)</note>, a little world, which has within itself and carries the figure of the Cross. <margin>Caelius Rhodiginus.</margin>
Caelius Rhodiginus <note>Ludovico Ricchieri (1469–1525), an Italian scholar known for his vast encyclopedia of ancient knowledge.</note>, in the 8th Chapter of the 6th book of his *Ancient Lessons* <note>original: "Leçons anticques," referring to his work 'Antiquarum lectionum'.</note>, gives many other good and beautiful reasons for the Cross, which I leave out for the sake of brevity, referring good students who wish to enjoy them further to that source.

I will stick to the reason I have stated: that the Cross, insofar as it is made of a perpendicular and a horizontal line, is the foundation for designing all our aforementioned Attic letters, as I shall show by example and illustration hereafter, our Lord helping.

The reason why one writes three As, rather than two or four, is once again a sign of happiness <note>The author uses "happiness" (felicité) here in the sense of divine favor or auspiciousness.</note>, for the number of the Trinity is an <term>odd number</term> <note>original: "nombre Imper." From the Latin 'impar', meaning odd.</note>, and among all other numbers it is the most noble and perfect. It is composed of both even and odd numbers, yet the total itself is odd. Virgil said in his *Bucolics*: "God delights in an odd number" <note>original: "Numero Deus impare gaudet." From Virgil's Eclogue VIII.</note>. Divine things, he says, desire to be in an odd number. Thus we also have in our good and holy faith the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. All three of whom we believe to be one Deity and of equal power. In the same way, our three As have but one Virtue in syllable and speech. To show us this blessed Trinity and joyous repetition, the good Prophet Jeremiah in his first Chapter left us an example in writing when he said: "A, A, A, Lord God, behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am but a child" <note>original: "A, A, A, domine, Deus, ecce, nescio loqui, quia puer ego sum." A, A, A, he says, my Lord God: you see that I cannot speak because I am but a child. When a child is born, the first voice it produces contains within it—so it is said—this letter A; and for this reason our good ancient fathers placed it first in the rank of letters, rather than M, or S, or any other of all the letters. One could still provide many other good reasons for this matter, but whoever desires to know them in full should read Plutarch in his *Symposiacs*, Ninth Decade <note>original: "In simposiacis. Decade nona." Referring to Plutarch's 'Table Talk' (Quaestiones Conviviales), where the origins of the alphabet are discussed.</note>, and there he may satisfy his mind, if it is a mind easily satisfied.

# On the Proportion of Letters

<margin>The Apocalypse.</margin>
...the penultimate chapter of the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>: "I am Alpha and Omega" <note>original: *Ego sum Alpha et $\omega$*</note>. That is to say in Latin: "I am the beginning and the end" <note>original: *Ego sum initium & finis*</note>. And in French: "I am the beginning and the end." Likewise in the final chapter: "I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end" <note>original: *Ego sum Alpha & $\omega$, primus & nouissimus, principium & finis*</note>. I am, says he, Alpha and Omega; that is to say the first and the last, I am the beginning and the end. Alpha, then, is used for the "beginning," and for this reason A is placed first in the alphabetical order, a subject which may be seen in Plato, who discusses it.
<margin>Plato.</margin>

<margin>Alphabetical letters in Greek serve as number signs.</margin>
There is yet another secret reason why Alpha signifies the beginning. And that is that the Greeks count and form their numbers by their letters. Their said letters—as is also done in Hebrew—serve them as ciphers and signs of numbers for counting. Alpha (A) is used for the first number, and for one. <term>Beta</term> <note>original: *Vita*. This spelling reflects the Byzantine pronunciation common during the Renaissance, where the Greek letter Beta was pronounced like a 'V'.</note> (B) is used for two. Gamma ($\Gamma$) for three. Delta ($\Delta$) for four. Epsilon (E) for five. But after the said Epsilon, $\varsigma$—that is to say, <term>Stigma</term> <note>original: *Sigma. Taf*. The author is describing the ligature of the letters Sigma and Tau, which was used in the Greek numbering system to represent the number 6.</note>—are placed together and signify six. And then Zeta (Z) is used for seven. Eta (H) for eight. Theta ($\Theta$) for nine. Iota (I) for ten. After this, Iota and Alpha (IA) together are used for eleven. Iota and Beta (IB) for twelve. And consequently so on with the other letters and certain insertions <note>The author refers here to archaic letters like *Koppa* and *Sampi* which were kept in the numbering system to represent 90 and 900.</note> that I omit for the sake of brevity.

Alpha, in the second book of the *Epigrams* of Martial, is also used—as has been said regarding the order of Greek letters—to mean the principal and the first, where he has written:

That is to say: "Lysimachus, I have today begun to go to school; I already know three letters: A, M, O." <note>The letters A, M, and O spell 'amo' in Latin, which means 'I love,' creating a play on words about the character's newfound 'education.'</note>

The A, joined with another vowel, makes a <term>Diphthong</term>. That is to say, a syllable containing within itself two vowels; this occurs in both Greek and Latin, but in French I find more than two vowels together in a single syllable and diphthong, as I could easily prove if I did not wish to move on for the sake of brevity.

### Book Three

<margin>A notable and very beautiful teaching.</margin>
I would have well begun with the point and the line, which are, as I have said before at the beginning of the second book, the foundation of every figure in commensuration <note>Commensuration refers to the measurement and proportion of parts relative to a whole—the "common measure."</note>, but I wished to begin with the cross, for the reasons I have stated previously. The square that you see after the said cross is the arena and exercise ground for our studious design in making each of our said Attic letters <note>original: "lettres Atticques." Tory uses "Attic" to refer to classical Roman capitals, linking them to the artistic refinement of ancient Greece.</note>. You see there eleven perpendicular lines and as many crossing in a cross, which yield ten times ten small squares, coming to a total number of one hundred. The width of one [square], as I have said, is for the width of the leg <note>In modern typography, we call this the "stem" or the main stroke of the letter.</note> of the letter that you wish to make. And notably, observe that when it pleases you to want to make an Attic letter, you must before all things establish a square according to the height you intend to make it, then mark a cross in the middle, and consequently the other lines on one side and the other in equidistant measure, so that the said square is equally divided, as I have said, into eleven perpendicular lines and as many crossing ones. Or, if you wish to do better, make your cross and then around it your said square divided proportionately, as I have already said several times.

<margin>*Radius* <note>original Latin: "Radius," meaning a rod, staff, or the spoke of a wheel; here it refers to a measuring tool or ruler.</note></margin>
Thus, therefore, upon a square divided as above, we shall make our first letter A: but to agree with what I have written before, we shall make it in three sorts, which will be three A's; one will be black and upright, the other will be white and inverted, and the third will be [made] of a compass and a ruler, which is called in Latin, *Radius*, to show that every Attic letter must be made with the compass and the ruler.

# Book Three

<margin>The A, made of a compass and a ruler.</margin>
<margin>A noteworthy point on the compass and the ruler.</margin>
Following my previous words, I have here designed and proportioned an A, in which, by harmonious accord, a compass and a ruler are represented. Or, if you prefer to put it another way, say that I have made an A out of a compass and a ruler, according to the <term>secret doctrine|A common Renaissance idea that ancient knowledge was hidden in symbols and required special study to uncover</term> of the good ancients. To lead us toward making the <term>Attic letter|Tory’s term for the classical Roman capital letter, which he associated with Greek (Attic) purity</term> correctly, they established the first of their letters in the shape and representation of the two most certain tools that are necessary and required to well-construct not only the Attic letter, but also <term>blackletter|original: "lettre de forme," referring to the heavy, gothic styles common in early printing</term> and every other kind. Among all manual tools, the compass is the King and the ruler is the Queen; that is to say, they are the two most noble and sovereign, under which all other tools—and all things well-ordered and duly made—find their reason.

<margin>Good advice.</margin>
<margin>Mention of the Italians.</margin>
I would have cause here to speak and write the praises and perfections of the said compass and ruler, but I will leave that for someone more studious than I to spend their time upon. I will say nothing more of it for now, except that no man will ever write well in the Attic letter, nor in any other letter, without a compass and without a ruler; and that in all things where there is no due proportion—which is found beneath the compass and ruler—there is neither order nor reason. Therefore, lords and devoted lovers of knowledge, love the compass and the ruler, recreating and exercising yourselves in them to know the reason and truth of good things. The <note>Tory often looked to Italian Renaissance masters like Leonardo or Pacioli as both inspiration and rivals</note> Italians, who are masters in perspective, painting, and <term>imagery|original: "imagerie," referring here to the art of sculpture or the creation of lifelike figures</term>, always have the compass and the ruler in hand; thus, they are the most perfect at rendering things precisely and representing

# Of the Proportion of Letters

<margin>Leonardo da Vinci.

...naturalness, and in making shadows as well as any known in Christendom. They have, moreover, a grace, for they are cool-headed and studious, with sobriety in drinking, eating, and speaking lightly, and in not finding themselves too quickly in company; in doing which they learn more surely and better, and give themselves a reputation, which they do not consider a small thing. We do not have as many such beautiful virtues in this area <note>Tory refers to France or northern Europe</note> as they have; likewise, we see none on this side of the Alps who are to be compared to the late Sir Leonardo da Vinci, to Donatello, to Raphael of Urbino, nor to Michelangelo. I do not mean to say that there are not beautiful and good spirits among us, but there is still a failure to continue using the compass and the ruler.

I return to my A, made from a compass and a ruler, and I pray those reading this little work that they do not think I have thus devised and made it to create a rebus for them, or to make them dream <note>Tory uses "resuer" (to dream/rave) to mean wasting time on idle or nonsensical speculation</note> over it, but to advise them by reasonable discourse, and to show them clearly <note>original: "au doigt & à l'œil" — literally "to the finger and the eye," a French idiom meaning to demonstrate something with absolute clarity</note> that the true Attic letter, as I have said, must necessarily be made with the ruler and the compass.

<margin>Recapitulation.</margin>

<margin>Leonardo da Vinci.</margin>
<margin>Sigismondo Fanti of Ferrara.</margin>
Which is to say in English: "This letter A is drawn from its circle and its square. The right-hand leg must be as thick as one of the nine parts of its height." He divides his square into only nine parts, and provides no reasoning for it yet; therefore, subject to correction, it seems to me that he speaks of it like an unlearned man <note>original: "clerc d'armes" — literally "clerk of arms," a term for someone who pretends to have knowledge they do not actually possess</note>, erring from the very first letter, and consequently in all the others. I have heard that everything he has done, he secretly took from the late Sir Leonardo da Vinci, who was a great mathematician, painter, and sculptor <note>original: "imageur" — a maker of images or statues</note>. Sigismondo Fanti, a nobleman of Ferrara, who, as I have said before, strives to teach the writing of various types of letters, gives no reason for the proportion of his said various types of letters, and especially for the Antique letter <note>The "Antique" letter refers to what we now call Roman capitals</note>. He has also erred in the A, the E, the L, the Q, S, T, and the X, which are made neither with the measurement nor in the manner they require. The keen eye of the learned and studious man will easily be able to recognize this in the book that the said Sigismondo has had printed, titled *Thesaurus for Writers* <note>original: "Thesauro de Scrittori"</note>.

# On the Proportion of Letters

<margin>Mention of the Gascons.</margin>
BARBARIAN <note>original: "ΒΑΡΒΑΡΟΣ". The term implies a foreigner or someone whose speech is unintelligible.</note>. *Varuaros*, *Babai*, *vauæ*. <note>Tory is likely imitating the sounds of babbling or foreign phonemes.</note> The Gascons <note>people from the Gascony region in southwest France</note> maintain this pronunciation in their language in many of their utterances, such as when they wish to say: "I have drunk [beu] some good wine," they say: "I have seen [veu] some good bin." Likewise in Latin: *Man does not drink [bibit] by bread alone*, instead of, *Man lives [vivit]*. <note>Tory is referencing a common Renaissance joke about the linguistic confusion between the Latin 'v' and 'b' in the Iberian and Gascon regions: "Happy are the people for whom to live (vivere) is to drink (bibere)."</note> And in saying this, the meaning is very often perverted according to proper French and according to Latin, as you see in the aforementioned examples cited, where instead of "I have drunk," there is "I have seen," and for "lives," there is "drinks." They commit many other incongruities, as when they say: "A calf [veau] old man," for "A handsome [beau] old man." In place of the consonant V they say B, and in place of B, they say the consonant V.

<margin>Mu before Pi.</margin>
When Mu <note>original: "My"</note> in Greek—that is to say M—is before Pi <note>original: "Py"</note>—that is to say before P—the Pi is pronounced as the Latins and we pronounce the B. These same Greeks write LAMP <note>original: "ΛΑΜΠΑΣ"</note> and I SEND <note>original: "ΠΕΜΠΩ"</note> with a Pi, and pronounce them *Lambas* and *Pembo*.

<margin>P into B.
B into the consonant V.
Mention of the Gascons.</margin>
The Gascons do not only pronounce B for the consonant V in French, but similarly in Latin, as when they say: *Good day* <note>original: "vona dies" for "Bona dies"</note>. *May he drink happily* <note>original: "Bibat faustus" for "Vivat faustus"</note>. *Come to me and you shall drink* <note>original: "Beni ad me & bibes" for "Veni ad me & bibes"</note>, because they have the consonant V in such frequent usage. It seems that the Latins called them *Vascones* <note>Basques/Gascons</note> with a V, rather than *Gascones*, to secretly give some understanding of this.

<margin>Mention of the Germans.</margin>
I have also seen Germans <note>original: "Alemans"</note> who pronounced P for B when they spoke in French; as when wanting to say: "There is a very fine and good beast," they said: "There is a very pine pine and poon peste." <note>original: "pien pelle & ponne peſte"</note> This vice is common among them.

# On the Proportion of Letters

The chapter *On the exchange of letters* <note>original Latin: "De literarum commutatione"</note> states:
*V* changes into *E*, as in *Weight* <note>original: "Pondus"</note> and *of weight* <note>original: "ponderis"</note>. [Also] *He swears an oath* <note>original: "Deierat"</note> and *He perjures* <note>original: "Peierat"</note> instead of *Deiurat* and *Peiurat*. *Lip* <note>original: "Labrum"</note> becomes *little lip* <note>original: "Labellum"</note>. *Sacred* <note>original: "Sacrum"</note> becomes *shrine* <note>original: "sacellum"</note>. The ancients used to say *Auget* and *Augeratus* instead of *Augur* <note>a religious official who interpreted omens</note> and *Auguratus* <note>the office of the Augur</note>.

<margin>The author of the Book of the Game of Chess</margin>
The letter *E* has three different sounds in French pronunciation and rhyme, as the author of the *Book of the Game of Chess* <note>likely referring to a version of Jacques de Cessoles' work, which often included moral or grammatical digressions</note> very elegantly teaches in the chapter where he treats the quality of rhymes. There, he speaks as follows: "We must know that this vowel which is called *E* can vary its sound, or be pronounced in three ways, even though we have only a single figure, or a single letter, that represents all three ways to us. 

The first way is when it is pronounced in its straight, perfect, principal, and first sound, as we commonly name it; for example, when we say *beauty* <note>French: "beauté"</note> or *loyalty* <note>French: "loyauté"</note>. 

The second way is when, in pronouncing it, one extends it to the side of the aforementioned straight sound; as when we say *Morning* <note>French: "Matinée"</note> or *Robine* <note>likely a feminine name or diminutive</note>, and other similar words. And in these cases, the aforementioned vowel causes the number and the measure of the rhyme to vary, because the sound is in itself full and perfect. And thus, it holds and occupies the place of an entire syllable. 

And the third way is when, in pronouncing the aforementioned vowel, it does not sound like a full vowel but rather flows and loses its sound, as it were. Such as when we say *Nature*, *Creature*, *Villainy* <note>French: "Villennie"</note>, or *Felony* <note>French: "Felonie"</note>; and in many other different ways. And in this case, the aforementioned vowel thus pronounced does not vary the number of the preceding syllables, nor—"

<margin>Mention of the Germans.</margin>
The Germans have this custom of pronunciation—though not in writing—of saying and uttering F in place of V when it is a consonant, at least when they speak in Latin. If they wanted to say: *I drank old wine* <note>original: "Ego bibi vinum vetus."</note>, they would pronounce it: *Eio bibi finum fetus*. This manner of pronouncing is peculiar and common to them; for the Latins, whom they ought to follow, do not pronounce it thus. 

<margin>Priscian.</margin>
It seems that the said Germans maintain such pronunciation because Priscian <note>A 6th-century Latin grammarian whose "Institutes of Grammar" was the standard textbook for centuries.</note> left it in writing in his first book, stating: *Furthermore, this letter F has the sound that V now has when it is placed in the position of a consonant.* <note>original: "Habet autem hæc F, litera hunc sonum quem nunc habet V, loco consonantis posita."</note>

# On the proportion of letters

The letter G, depicted here, is constructed from an O and a truncated I <note>Tory views letters as being built out of two primary shapes: the circle (O) and the straight line (I).</note>; it is nine and a half "bodies" <note>body: a unit of measurement in Tory’s grid system, where the height of the letter is divided into ten parts.</note> in width, and requires eight turns of the compass to create. For this reason, I have marked eight centers in their proper places.

<margin>Master Simon Hayeneufue.</margin>
Master Simon Hayeneufue, who is commonly called Master Simon of Le Mans, makes a small half-circle at the bottom of the short leg of the G, which gives it a very fine grace. However, I have seen it in the galleries of Pope Julius II <note>Pope Julius II (reigned 1503–1513) was a massive patron of the arts, commissioning Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel ceiling.</note>, between the Palace of Saint Peter and the Belvedere, cut at a perpendicular line; therefore, make it however you please. The aforementioned Master Simon is the greatest and most excellent workman in ancient architecture <note>Meaning the "Classical" Roman style which was being rediscovered during the Renaissance.</note> known to me among the living. He is a man of the church and of good life, friendly and helpful to everyone regarding designs and portraits in the true ancient style. He makes these so well that if Vitruvius <note>A Roman architect (1st century BC) whose writings were the "bible" of Renaissance architecture.</note> or Leon Battista Alberti <note>A 15th-century Italian humanist and architect who codified the rules of perspective and classical design.</note> were alive, they would grant him the prize over any of those on this side of the mountains <note>original: "deça les monts" — this refers to artists in France and Northern Europe, as opposed to Italy.</note>. In Greek, G is called Gamma; but as I have said before, that Gamma is different in shape, for it is made as if an L were turned so that the bottom was placed at the top, in this fashion: Γ. G and Gamma have similar

<margin>Rule of orthography.</margin>
phonetic power in syllables, except that Gamma, when written before another Gamma, or before Chi (Χ), or before Kappa (Κ), or before Xi (ξ), is pronounced as "ng"—that is to say, as an N. # On the proportion of letters

<note>original: "gordius erat insolubilis"</note> the Gordian knot was insoluble. And, a *gutturnium* <note>original: "Gutturnium est vas guttatim stilans"</note> is a vessel that drips drop by drop. They <note>The Germans, mentioned on the previous page.</note> would say: *Iaudeamus*, *iordius*, *iutturnium*, and *iuttatim*: which would seem like words outside of true Latinity. Before E, and before I, they pronounce it well, saying: *Germinavit radix Jesse* <note>The root of Jesse has blossomed; a common biblical reference.</note>. *Gigis annulus erat fatalis* <note>The ring of Gyges was fated; referring to the mythical ring of invisibility belonging to Gyges of Lydia.</note>. But, as I have said, before A, O, and V, they do not pronounce it in a sufficiently Latin manner.

<margin>G for C, and C for G.</margin>
G has a great affinity with C, so much so that very often it is pronounced where the C is written: as we see in these words, *Cneus*, and *Caius* <note>Names of prominent Romans, now usually spelled Gnaeus and Gaius.</note>, which are written with C and pronounced with G. There are other words in which the G is written and pronounced in place of the C, such as *quadringenta* <note>Four hundred</note> and *quingenta* <note>Five hundred</note>, instead of *quadrincenta* and *quincenta*.

<margin>Mention of Bourges.</margin>
The affinity of G for C, and C for G, is observed a bit too much in Bourges, where I was born: for there are those who pronounce *Ignem* <note>Fire</note>, *lignum* <note>Wood</note>, and other similar words, as if a C were written in place of the G, pronouncing them *Icnem* and *licnum*. This should not be pronounced this way according to the Latin language; for the Italians pronounce the G very softly when it is between I and N.

<margin>Mention of the Picards.</margin>
The Picards <note>People from Picardy, a region in northern France.</note>, contrary to the aforementioned Germans (who pronounce the consonant I for G), pronounce the G in place of the consonant I <note>In 16th-century French, 'I' was often used where we now use 'J'.</note> in certain words. For example, instead of saying: "Ma iambe s'est rompue en nostre iardin, et y ay perdu mon chapeau iaulne" <note>"My leg broke in our garden, and I lost my yellow hat there."</note>, they say: "Me gambe s'est rompue en noz gardin, et y ay perdu men capiau gaulne." They say many others, which I leave out for the sake of brevity.

# Book Three

<margin>Mention of jokesters.</margin>
Jokesters and young lovers who delight in inventing <term>devises</term> <note>An emblem or heraldic badge consisting of an image and a short motto.</note>, or in usurping them as if they had invented them themselves, use this letter G and an A to create a whimsical <term>devise</term>. They make the A <margin>Mention of rebuses.</margin> smaller than the G and place it inside the said G to form a <term>rebus</term> <note>A puzzle where pictures or letters represent words or sounds.</note>, and then they say that it means: "I have a big appetite" <note>original: "I'ay grand appetit" — In French, the letter G is pronounced like "J'ai" (I have), "grand" means big, and "A petit" (small A) sounds like "appétit" (appetite).</note>. In this matter, neither the spelling nor the pronunciation is at all appropriate, but I forgive them, leaving them to their jokes in their youthful loves. <margin>Large G, small A.</margin> The said large G and small A are intended to be in the manner that follows.

<margin>
They make many others from diverse letters, such as K, V, K, A, B, and "go away, L" <note>These phonetic strings form sentences: "K-V-K-A-B" sounds like "qu'as-tu qu'a bée" (what do you have that is gaping?) and "L" sounds like "Elle" (She).</note>. XX. L, X NA. L, was N <note>"X N A" sounds like "Dix en a" (He has ten of them) and "L fut N" sounds like "Elle fut née" (She was born).</note>.
</margin>

<margin>Diverse rebuses.</margin>

"L went away" <note>original: "L, s'en alla" — sounds like "Elle s'en alla" (She went away).</note>. "G above L" <note>original: "G, ſus L" — G (J'ai) over L (elle), meaning "I have her."</note>, "my heart is bolted" <note>original: "mon cœur à VI" — The numeral VI (six) sounds like "vis" (a screw or bolt).</note>. "What do you wait for? Wait no more." "It is turned wrongly; a donkey would bite it" <note>A proverbial expression used to describe something so nonsensical or poorly constructed that it looks like bundles of straw or fodder.</note>. Likewise: "Peace, an I, green, saddle" <note>original: "Paix vn I, vert ſelle" — Phonetically "Paix-y-en-selle," a rebus for "Patience."</note>, which is made of a peace-sign, an I, the color green, and a saddle. In such foolish things, good <term>orthography</term> <note>The conventional spelling system of a language.</note> and true pronunciation are perverted.
