<margin>Writing made through images was invented by the Egyptians.</margin>
This manner of fanciful invention—that is to say, writing made through images—was first invented by the Egyptians, who had all their ceremonies written in this way so that the common people and the ignorant could not understand or easily know their secrets and mysteries. These writings were called in Greek *Hieroglyphics* <note>original: "Hieroglyphica"</note>, which is to say, *sacred writings* <note>original: "sacra scripta"</note>. Sacred writings that no one could understand without being a great Philosopher and one who could know the reason and virtues of natural things. When they wanted to signify the year, they designated and made a portrait or painting of a Dragon biting its tail <note>The Ouroboros, an ancient symbol of infinity and the cyclical nature of time.</note>. To signify liberality <note>Generosity.</note>, they made an open right hand. And for stinginess, a closed hand. The foliage and the flowers that are on the said pot signify the virtues that our body could have within itself during its life. # On the Proportion of Letters

...deep from the stomach. This same Priscian says: "H, however, is a mark of aspiration, and has nothing else of the quality of a letter except for its shape, and the fact that by custom it is written among other letters." <note>original Latin: "H, autem aſpirationis est nota, & nihil aliud habet literæ, niſi figuram, & quod in uſu ſcribitur inter alias literas."</note> That is to say, H is the mark of aspiration, and has no other functional power as a letter, save for its shape, and also that it is written by convention.

<margin>$\Theta. \Phi. X. \text{P}.$</margin>
<margin>Aldus.</margin>
**H** has so little power when paired with vowels that if it is removed, the meaning is not diminished; however, it has a great deal of power when paired with the four aforementioned consonants: C, P, R, and T. Example with vowels: *Ereñius* [Herennius], *Oratius* [Horatius]. <note>Tory notes that in Latin, omitting the H in these names does not fundamentally change the word's identity.</note> Example with the said consonants: *Cremes* instead of *Chremes*. And for this reason, as Priscian says in the previously cited passage, the Greeks created these aforementioned aspirated consonants. For instead of Th, they made $\Theta$ [Theta]; for Ph, $\Phi$ [Phi]; for Ch, $\text{X}$ [Chi]. The Rho [$\text{P}$] was not changed in its shape, but it takes upon itself a half-cross in capital letters, or a curved point <note>A rough breathing mark ( ̔).</note> in cursive script which denotes the said aspiration, as can be clearly seen in the printed works of the late, good printer Aldus, <note>Aldus Manutius (1449–1515), the famous Venetian printer known for his beautiful Greek type and the "Anchor and Dolphin" mark.</note> may God rest his soul.

<margin>Aulus Gellius.</margin>
**A**ulus Gellius, <note>A 2nd-century Roman author whose "Attic Nights" is a collection of observations on grammar, philosophy, and history.</note> in the fourth chapter of the second book of his *Attic Nights*, says that H was used by the ancients and inserted into words to give them a firmer and more vigorous sound, when he says: "The letter H—whether it should be called a breath rather than a letter—our ancestors used to insert into many words to strengthen and bolster them, so that their sound might be fresher and more vigorous. And they seem to have done this out of a study and imitation of the Attic language. It is well enough known that the Attics [used the breath for] *ichthyn* [fish] and *aera* [air]. <note>original Greek: ἰχϑὺν ἠέϱ. Gellius refers to the Greek practice of adding a "rough breathing" to the start of words.</note> Likewise, they said many other things contrary to the custom of the other nations of Greece, by breathing upon the first letter; thus *lachrymas* [tears], thus *speculum* [mirror], thus *ahenum* [bronze], thus *vehemens* [vehement], thus *inchoare* [to begin], thus *helluari* [to gluttonize], thus *hal-* [to breathe]..."

...hallucinate, so they said *honera* [burdens], so *honustum* [laden]. In all these words, no reason for this letter or breath was seen, except that the firmness and vigor of the voice might be intensified, as if by adding certain sinews. <note>original Latin: "lucinari, ſic honera, ſic honuſtum dixerunt. In his verbis omnibus literae ſeu ſpiritus iſtius nulla ratio viſa eſt, niſi vt firmitas & vigor vocis quaſi quibuſdam neruis additis intenderetur."</note> That is to say, the letter H—or if it is better to call it the vocal breath—was often inserted by the ancient Latins into many words to strengthen and reinforce them, so that their sound would be more potent and vigorous. These ancients did this in imitation of the Athenians, in whose language *to live as a private citizen* <note>original Greek: "ἰδωυεῖν", likely a transcription of ἰδιωτεύειν (idioteuein).</note> and many similar words were aspirated, contrary to the custom of the other nations of Greece. Thus were aspirated: *Tears* [Lachrymae], *Mirror* [spechulum], *Bronze* [ahenum], *Vehement* [vehemens], *To begin* [inchoare], *To hallucinate* [hallucinari], *Burdens* [honera], and *Laden* [honustus]. In these aforementioned vowels, the aspiration was not seen as having a logical reason, except to give them firmness and vigor, as if they were strengthened by sinews.

<margin>A unique and noteworthy point.</margin>
**T**he Romans modeled this mark of aspiration entirely on the figure and form of a Greek vowel named Eta [H]. <note>Tory uses "Ita," reflecting the Erasmian or Reuchlinian pronunciation debates of the Renaissance; he is referring to the Greek letter Eta (Η).</note> The Greeks made from their said vowel Eta, H, two passive marks similar to accents, to show when an initial vowel, and the consonant Rho—also when initial or doubled in the composition of a noun or verb—should be aspirated or not. For by cutting the said vowel Eta exactly through the middle into two perpendicular parts, 

<margin>H. Ⱶ ⱶ signs of aspiration and of the non-aspirated letter.</margin>
the first part [Ⱶ] serves to show the aspirated vowel or the consonant Rho, and the other part [ⱶ] for the vowel or Rho that is not aspirated. The said Greek vowel Eta is divided thus: Ⱶ and ⱶ, and its parts are written above aspirated letters. <note>These two halves of the capital H are the ancestors of the "rough breathing" ( ̔) and "smooth breathing" ( ̓) marks used in Greek typography to indicate whether a word starts with an 'h' sound.</note>

The resemblance between this aforementioned Latin aspiration <note>The letter H.</note> and the Greek vowel *ita* <note>Tory refers to the Greek letter Eta (Η). In the Renaissance, pronunciation debates led some to call it "ita."</note> has been the cause of a thousand modern people, who are ignorant of the Greek language, wandering into error; they err every day in their orthography—that is to say, in the proper writing—of those two sovereign and precious names, *Jesus* and *Christ*. For in writing them in abbreviated form, they write *Ihesus* with a Latin aspiration, and *XPS* <note>original Greek: "ΧΡΣ"</note> with a Latin X and P. However, in Greek, *IHS* <note>original Greek: "ΙΗΣ"</note> should be written with the aforementioned vowel *ita* [Η], and *XPS* with *chi* [Χ] and *rho* [Ρ]. The error has come to them, as I said, because *ita* [Η] and the Latin aspiration [H] have a similar shape, and because *chi* [Χ] and *rho* [Ρ] also almost resemble a Latin X and P. Therefore, in this matter, I pray all good spirits that from now on, when they wish to write the most holy and glorious name and surname of our Savior, if they wish to write it

good and

Christians.
</margin>

When the Greek vowel *ita* [Η] is converted into Latin, it translates as a long E, for the length of the syllable, as in this glorious name, *IESOUS* <note>original Greek: "ΙΗΣΟΥΣ"</note>, *Iesus*, and in a thousand other similar cases. Therefore, one must write *Iesus* without an aspiration...

Likewise in the sixth:

> *Ah, unhappy maiden: what madness has seized you?* <note>original: "Ache virgo infelix: quæ te dementia cæpit?"</note>

This would entirely spoil the style and the metric quantity.

<margin>Spondee.</margin>
The phrase *...mo hic* <note>The end of the word 'Samo' and the beginning of 'hic'.</note> is a spondee. <image-desc>A geometric diagram of the capital letter 'I' inscribed within a 10x10 square grid. The letter consists of a vertical stem one unit wide. That is to say, three whole units, as in the head, and two halves on the two sides to give it a paw <note>A "patte," referring here to the serif or the spreading base of the letter.</note>, a seat, and a foundation to better support the said head. And the reason is taken from the nature of the human body: for when a man is on his feet, those feet are more spread out and wider than the space and width of his head. A man stands more firmly having his feet moderately wide apart than having them joined one against the other. Thus, our I should be wider at its foot than at its head.

<margin>The I is the model for all letters.</margin>

<margin>Martianus Capella. Mention of the Flemings. Iota.</margin>

<margin>
C, D, Q,

letters

Therefore, I say that there are eight letters that serve as numbers: namely, two vowels, **I** and **V**; two semi-vowels, **L** and **M**; three mutes, **C**, **D**, and **Q**; and one double consonant, **X**. The **I** alone is set for one; when it is doubled, it is worth two. When it is tripled, it makes three; and when it is quadrupled, it signifies four. And note that it is no longer multiplied by itself beyond that. It is multiplied with the other aforementioned letters, and this only up to four times.

# On the proportion of letters

<margin>Mention of the Cappadocians, the Cretans, and the Cilicians.</margin>
...in Greece, there were three nations of a very malicious nature, and these were the Cappadocians, the Cretans, and the Cilicians, who were all and always cunning and accustomed to every kind of deceit. Regarding the *tria Cappa* <note>original: "tria Cappa," meaning "Three Kappas." This refers to a Greek proverb warning against the three ethnic groups beginning with K.</note> turned into a Greek proverb, I saw in Rome a gentleman and a pleasant lover, who (as those in these parts often do for the love <margin>Beatrice.</margin> of their lady) wore as his device a **B**, an **A**, and three **C**s, written thus: **B, A, CCC.** And by this, he intended the name of his lady-love, who was called **Beatrice**. This name is pronounced in the Italian vernacular as if the **C** were aspirated, and as if one should write it **Beatriche** <note>Tory is explaining that the "tri-C" (three Cs) sounds like "trice" or "triche" in Italian phonetics.</note>.

I say this in passing to show that **K** should be pronounced sharp and pure, yet the sharpness should be a bit soft, almost as if it were aspirated.

<margin>Mention of the Kappa and the Chi.</margin>
The Greeks never aspirate their Kappa, **K**, but they have another letter in its place which carries its aspiration, and is named **Chi**. It is equivalent to **C** and **H**, so that if they wished to write *Cha, che, chi, cho,* or *chu*, they would write: **χα, χε, χι, χο,** and **χυ** <note>original: "cha, che, chi, cho, chu" in Greek script.</note>. I leave the exercise and enjoyment of such matters to those of noble spirit.

The letter **L**, designed hereafter, is ten "bodies" <note>Tory uses "corps" or "bodies" as his standard unit of measurement for proportions.</note> in height and seven and a half in width. For its perfection, five turns of the compass are required, and to do this, I have marked five crosses in the places where it is appropriate to set the foot of said compass.

# On the Proportion of Letters

<margin>Martianus Capella.</margin>
Martianus Capella says that the letter L "sweetens with the tongue and the palate." <note>original: "linguæ palato'que dulcescit." Martianus Capella was a 5th-century Roman author known for his work on the Seven Liberal Arts.</note> That is to say, L must be pronounced with the tongue and the palate—which is the upper concavity of the mouth—with a soft breath of voice. In this phonetic description, its physical form is also understood: it consists of a perpendicular line forming an angle at its heel, upon which it sits.

<margin>Priscian. Pliny.</margin>
Priscian, in the first book of his work, in the chapter *On the Interchange of Letters*, says that Pliny was of the opinion that L contained three distinct sounds in pronunciation.

<margin>Priscian.</margin>
The words of the said Priscian are as follows:
*L (as it seemed to Pliny) has a triple sound: Slender, when it is doubled in the second position, as in: Ille, Metellus. Full, when it ends names or syllables, or when it has a consonant before it in the same syllable: as in Sol (Sun), sylua (forest), flauus (yellow), clarus (clear). However, it is medium in others: as in lectus (bed), lectum (read).* <note>original: "L, triplicem (vt Plinio videtur) sonum habet: Exilem, quādo geminatur secundo loco posita, vt, Ille, Metellus. Plenum, quando finit nomina, vel syllabas, & quando habet ante se in eadem syllaba aliquam consonantem. vt Sol, sylua, flauus, clarus. Mediū autē in aliis. vt lectus lectū."</note>

<margin>The letter L has three sounds in pronunciation.</margin>
That is to say, L has three types of sounds (as it seemed to Pliny). The first sound is slender and simple in sweetness, and this occurs when the letter is double or paired, as in saying: *Ille* and *Metellus*. The second sound is called the "full" sound; this occurs when it finishes and ends words or syllables, or when it is preceded by a consonant in the same syllable: as in saying: *Sol, sylua, flauus, clarus*. The third and last sound is "medium"; this occurs when the letter is found in other positions in syllables or words not described in the first two categories.

<margin>A singular note for the pronunciation of letters.</margin>
Whoever wishes to pronounce it well should utter it as if they meant to say this syllable: EL. And on this subject, I wish in this place to teach the just and proper pronunciation of all the letters of the alphabet, in which matter I see a thousand people err, when they say: A, boy, çoy, doy, ouy. <note>Tory is criticizing a contemporary trend where speakers pronounced the names of letters like B, C, and D with an "oy" sound (like "boy") instead of the standard "be, ce, de."</note>

...[Rhodiginus] says that it is the letter T which should be called and understood in the works of Plautus as the **long letter** <note>original: *Litera longa*</note>, though it seems to me he has little reason for this. <margin>Ancient proverb.</margin>
That there is no one so good that they do not err sometimes, just as it is said that Homer erred in certain passages of his poetic works.

# Book Three.

<margin>Martianus Capella.</margin>
"M," says Martianus Capella <note>A 5th-century Latin author known for an influential work on the seven liberal arts.</note>, "is pressed with the lips." That is to say, M must be pronounced in such a way that in uttering it—and its sound consists of this in effect—one must press, that is to say, squeeze the two lips together, without the tongue being moved, nor touching the front teeth, nor on any side whatsoever.

<margin>M. Half-sound. Galeotus.</margin>
<margin>Priscian.</margin>
<margin>M has three sounds.</margin>
The shape of the M is exactly the same for both the Greeks and the Latins; and it is named in Greek *Mu* <note>original: "My"</note>, which is as much as to say M, which should be pronounced with an imperfect sound, almost withdrawn into the mouth, as when saying "em." For this reason, some ancients formerly called it *Hemitonium* <term>Hemitonium: from Greek, meaning "half-tone," referring to a muted or semi-vocalized sound</term>. That is to say, a letter with a half-sound. Concerning this matter, Galeotus Martius of Narni <note>Galeotto Marzio (1427–1497), an Italian humanist scholar and physician.</note> is a witness in his second book titled *On the Inner Man* <note>original: "De homine interiori"</note>. Priscian <note>A famous 6th-century Latin grammarian whose work was a standard textbook in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note>, in the section where he treats *On the Mutation of Letters* <note>original: "De literarum commutatione"</note>, says that M has three types of sounds: obscure, open, and middling. His words are as follows: <note>Tory quotes Priscian in Latin: "m, obfcurum in extremitate dictionum fonat, vt templum. Apertum in pricipio, vt Magnus. Mediocre in medijs, vt vmbra."</note> "M sounds obscurely at the end of words, as in *templum* [temple]. It sounds open at the beginning, as in *Magnus* [Great]. It is middling in the middle, as in *umbra* [shadow]." M, he says, at the extremity and end of words sounds obscurely, as in this word *Templum*. It also has a sound at the beginning which is open, as in this word *Magnus*. Likewise, it has a middling sound in the middle, as in this word *vmbra*.

<margin>Mention of the Normans.</margin>
The Normans <note>People from the Normandy region of France, here cited for their specific regional accent when speaking Latin.</note> err in the proper pronunciation of this letter M when it is at the end of Latin words; for instead of *Templum* they say *Templun*, pronouncing N for M, and *Patren* for *Patrem* [Father], which does not follow the rule of Latin Grammar.

<margin>A notable point.</margin>
On this subject, because I see many speakers and many writers err regarding this said letter M—namely, by very often putting N...

# On the Proportion of Letters

...syllable, and sometimes long, and all this in one and the same written character. But in Greek, there is Omicron and Omega. That is to say, "short O" <note>original: *O, breue*</note> and "long O" <note>original: *O, longum*</note>.

<margin>
A singular and noteworthy point.
</margin>
Short O and long <note>original: *p̃duyt* (produit)</note> O are shown in two ways of writing. The Omicron is perfectly round on the outside uniformly, and the Latins <note>The "Latins" refers to the ancient Romans and those who use the Roman alphabet.</note> have adopted it without changing its shape. The Omega, as a capital letter, is round at the top and open at the bottom. Its form and true design are hardly well observed by some who write and pronounce this passage from the twenty-first and penultimate chapter of the Apocalypse <note>The Apocalypse refers to the biblical Book of Revelation.</note>, 

<margin>
Mention of the Apocalypse.
</margin>
where it is said, "I am the Alpha and the Omega" <note>original: *Ego fum Alpha & Ω*</note>. In this passage, instead of Omega (which should be made thus: Ω), they write a completely round O, which is an Omicron. Yet the meaning requires it to be Omega, which is the last letter of the Greek alphabet, for it is used there to signify completion and the end, saying: "I am the Alpha and the Omega." That is to say: "I am," says God, "the beginning and the completion of all good things." 

<margin>
Note this well, and pay close attention.
</margin>
Omicron does not signify completion; therefore it seems to me, under humble correction, that Ω is more appropriate there than O. Furthermore, since "Alpha" is written out in full and entirely, I would like to know if it would not also be good to write and say "Omega" as well? Thus: "I am the Alpha and the Omega" <note>original: *Ego fum Alpha & Omega*</note>. Since Alpha is written and pronounced in full, it seems likely to me that Omega should be so as 

<margin>
Good and devout souls, understand this well.
</margin>
well; or else, say and write: "I am A and Ω" <note>original: *Ego fum A, & Ω*</note>, so that A is no more written or pronounced in full than Ω. Καὶ τὸ. ω*</note>, using only simple letters A and Ω. <margin>Vocative adverb.</margin> O, in Greek, Latin, and French, is a vocative adverb <note>A part of speech used to address someone or something directly.</note>. ### Book Three.

<margin>Martianus Capella.</margin>
The **pronunciation** of this letter **Q** requires striking the tongue against the palate and narrowing the mouth, as *Martianus Capella* <note>A late Roman author whose work "The Marriage of Philology and Mercury" defined the seven liberal arts for the Middle Ages.</note> teaches when he says: *Q is formed by the pulse against the palate, with the mouth restricted* <note>original: "Q, appulsu palati, ore restricto."</note>. **Q**, he tells us, is pronounced by the touch of the tongue to the palate and by the narrowing of the mouth.

<margin>A singular notable point.</margin>
I have said previously in the second book that **Q** is the only letter among all the others that goes outside the line <note>Tory refers to the "descender" or tail of the Q, which breaks the baseline of the other capital letters</note>, and the reason is that it is never written in a word with other letters without immediately and closely following it with a **U**, which it goes to seek and embrace from underneath as its ordinary companion and loyal friend. 
<margin>All twenty-four Greek letters are always written between two equidistant lines.</margin>
**Q** is indeed sometimes used as an abbreviation all by itself with a period, and signifies the same as *Quintus* <note>A common Roman first name</note>. Similarly in French: Who is it?

<margin>Example in dialogue.</margin>
"Who is this?" "It is **Quentin**." "**What** does he want?" "He is looking for the street of **Quiquempoit** <note>Now known as Rue Quincampoix, a famous street in Paris</note>." "To do what?" "To find **someone** there, to go play **Skittles** [Quilles]."

**Q** and **C** are almost equal in shape and power, except that **Q** is completely round at the head, and **C** is open. This refers to the people of Eretria, who were mocked in antiquity for adding 'r' sounds to the ends of words.</note>

# Of the Proportion of Letters

<margin>A singular point of note.</margin>
I willingly offer this demonstration here, because I see a thousand people who unknowingly write the said letter S wider at the top than at the bottom.

<margin>Martianus Capella.</margin>
The S, says Martianus Capella <note>A 5th-century Latin author whose work *The Marriage of Philology and Mercury* was a standard textbook on the seven liberal arts.</note>, "creates a whistling sound with the teeth struck." <note>original: "sibillum facit dentibus verberatis"</note> That is to say, the S is pronounced by making a whistling sound between clenched teeth. In Greek it is called Sigma <note>original: "Σίγμα"</note>, and it is different in shape, for the Greeks write it almost like a reclining M, thus: Σ. They pronounce it strongly and solidly, almost as powerfully as when we pronounce two Ss. When they say *Mousa* <note>original: "Μοῦσα"; the Greek word for "Muse"</note>, they pronounce it "Mussa," and they never make it thin or soft between two vowels, as we do. If they wanted to say *Musa* <note>the Latin word for Muse</note> or *Philosophia* <note>Philosophy</note>, they would pronounce them "Mussa" and "Philossophia." And likewise everywhere it is found between two vowels.

<margin>Sigma. Σ.</margin>
<margin>Mention of the Greeks</margin>
The S is called by the said Greeks an *arktikón stoicheîon* <note>original: "ἀρκτικὸν στοιχεῖον"</note>. That is to say, an inceptive letter <note>A letter that can begin a word or syllable before other consonants.</note>, because it can be placed in both Greek and Latin before all the Mutes <term>Mutes: Consonants like p, b, t, d, k, g that cannot be sounded without a vowel</term>, and before the M, in a syllable or a word of one syllable, like these words here: *Sbennýō* <note>original: "Σβεννύω"; to quench</note>; *Spártē* <note>original: "Σπάρτη"; Sparta</note>; *Skêptron* <note>original: "Σκῆπτρον"; scepter</note>; *Stémma* <note>original: "Στέμμα"; wreath or garland</note>; *Sthénos* <note>original: "Σθένος"; strength</note>; *Sphínx* <note>original: "Σφίγξ"</note>; *Schêma* <note>original: "Σχῆμα"; shape or form</note>; *Smáragdos* <note>original: "Σμάραγδος"; emerald</note>. And in Latin: *Scutum* [shield], *Spatium* [space], *Stamen* [warp thread], *scribo* [I write], *strues* [heap], *Stlembus* [slow/clumsy], *splendidus* [shining]. ### Book Three.

...employ some noble spirit who will wish to help organize and subject the noble French language to a certain rule for speaking and writing properly, according to the power of the letters, syllables, and perfect utterances in the said French language. The S, furthermore, is called <margin>Monadikon</margin> <note>original: "Μοναδικόν"</note> by the Greeks. That is to say, solitary, because in the division of the semivowels <note>Consonants that have a vowel-like opening of the mouth, such as f, l, m, n, r, s, x.</note>, among whose number it is found, it remains all alone in its power. For all the others are divided into four Liquids, which are L, M, N, and R, and into two semivowels called Doubles in their power, which are X and Z. It is of such power in pronunciation and in metrical quantity that it is sometimes stable, and sometimes it vanishes and is lost, so little efficacy does it have. For this reason it is <margin>Asemon</margin> nicknamed by the Greeks *asemon* <note>original: "ἄσημον"</note>. That is to say, ignoble, and without efficacy. It is lost not only by itself, but it even causes its neighboring vowel to vanish, and very often causes the quantity of the vowel that precedes it to change, as one can clearly see in many passages in the Latin poets, from among whom I will cite some verses <margin>Ennius.</margin> by the ancient father of Latin poets named Ennius, whom Aulus Gellius cites in the fourth chapter of the twelfth book of his *Attic Nights*, when he says:

> *A learned, faithful, and pleasant man, eloquent, and with his own* <note>original: "Doctus, fidelis, suauis homo, facundus, suóque"</note>
> *lot content, and blessed, wise, speaking the right thing at the* <note>original: "Contentus, atque beatus, scitus, secunda loquens in"</note>
> *right time, agreeable, and a man of few words.* <note>original: "Tempore commodus, & verborum vir paucorum."</note>

Which verses are measured in their quantity in such a way that the S is lost in the manner that follows:
*Doctū’ fi, delis, ſauis ho, moſa, cundū’ ſu, oque*
*Contēn, t’ atque be, atus, ſcitū’ ſe, cunda lo, quens in.*
<note>Tory is demonstrating elision in Latin scansion, where the final 's' of "Doctus," "facundus," and "scitus" is ignored to maintain the poetic meter.</note>

<meta>This page continues Tory's technical examination of the letter S, specifically how its phonetic "instability" in classical poetry necessitates a special typographic mark. ### On the proportion of letters

<margin>A fine point worth noting.</margin>
I say and cite these things here so that, if it should happen that one must write in Attic letters <note>Tory refers here to "Attic letters" as the elegant, classical style of Roman capitals or Greek script used by ancient scholars.</note> such meters where the S ought to vanish, one could write them honorably and skillfully without including the said letter S in the place where it might be lost, and instead write a **hooked point** <note>The early term for an apostrophe.</note> above the place where it ought to be. This **hooked point**, being placed above the lines at the end of words, signifies that there is some vowel or the S removed by virtue of the quantity of the meter, or because of the vowel that escapes into the following syllable or word.

<margin>Priscian.</margin>
Priscian <note>A famous Latin grammarian (c. 500 AD) whose work was the foundation for medieval linguistic study.</note> is a good witness for us in the chapter, *On the changing of letters*, where he says that the S very often loses its power: *The S, in meter among the most ancient writers, frequently loses its force.* <note>original: "s, in metro apud vetustissimos vim suam frequenter amittit."</note>

<margin>Virgil</margin>
*Virgil in the eleventh book of the Aeneid.*
> Each one places’ his foot, but how narrow these things you see. <note>original: "Ponit’ pes sibi quisque , sed haec quam angustá videtis." The mark in "Ponit’" indicates a dropped letter.</note>

*The same author in the twelfth book.*
> That the men’ had come together and were deciding the matter with the sword. <note>original: "Inter se coiisse vir’ & decernere ferro."</note>

<margin>The word "Ne".</margin>
*Furthermore, when the conjunction "Ne" follows, the S is entirely removed with an apostrophe. For example: "viden’", "satin’", "vin’", for "videsne", "satisne", and "visne".* <note>These are shortened forms of "Do you see?", "Is it enough?", and "Do you wish?"</note> That is to say, S in the meter of ancient Poets very often loses its power, as in the eleventh book of Virgil’s *Aeneid*, where it says: *Each one places’ his foot, but how narrow these things you see.* And in the twelfth book following, where it says: *That the men’ had come together and were deciding the matter with the sword.*

<margin>The Apostrophe.</margin>
Similarly, when this Latin conjunction, *Ne*, follows the S, that S is entirely removed, and one marks above it—as I have said—a **hooked point**, which is called an *Apostrophus* <note>The Apostrophe.</note>. As when saying: *viden’*, *satin’*, *vin’*, for and in place of saying, *videsne*, *satisne*, and *visne*.

### Book Three

<margin>A mention of the ladies of Paris.</margin>
The ladies of Paris, for the most part, observe this poetic figure well by dropping the S at the end of many words. For example, instead of saying: "We have dined in a garden, and have eaten white and black plums, sweet and bitter almonds, soft figs, apples, pears, and gooseberries," <note>In 16th-century French, the plural 's' was starting to become silent in speech, a trend Tory notices among Parisian women.</note> they say and pronounce it: "We have dine in a garden, and have eaten white and black plum, sweet and bitter almond, soft fig, apple, pear, and gooseberry." This vice <note>Tory, ever the perfectionist, views this natural linguistic shift as a "vice" or error in pronunciation.</note> would be excusable for them, were it not that it passes from woman to man, and that it results in a total failure to pronounce perfectly when speaking.

<margin>Mention of the Boeotians.</margin>
It is no wonder that S sometimes loses its power, since quite often the Boeotians, who are a Greek nation, put an aspiration <note>An "aspiration" refers to a breathy 'h' sound.</note> in its place, saying *myha* for *musa* <note>original Greek: "$\mu\upsilon h \alpha$" for "$\mu\upsilon\sigma\alpha$". Here, the 's' in the middle of the word for "Muse" is replaced by an 'h' sound.</note>. Just as, quite to the contrary, the S is often found substituted for that same aspiration in Latin, as in the words: *semis* (half), *sex* (six), *septem* (seven), *se* (oneself), *si* (if), *sal* (salt), which are written in Greek with a **dasia** <term>dasia: also known as "rough breathing," this is a small mark placed over a Greek vowel to indicate it should be preceded by an 'h' sound.</term>. That is to say, by a **hooked point** which signifies the said aspiration, and which must be written above the Greek vowels and the letter Rho, as Priscian <note>A famous Latin grammarian from the 6th century.</note> testifies in his first book where he treats *On the changing of letters*, when he says:

<margin>Priscian.</margin>
> Indeed, the S is often placed in stead of an aspiration in those words we have taken from the Greeks, such as *semis, sex, septem, se, si, sal*. For *hemis, hex, hepta, he, hi, hals* <note>These are the Greek forms of the Latin words listed above; the Greek words start with an 'h' sound (aspiration) where the Latin uses an 's'.</note> have an aspiration at the beginning among them. Furthermore, the kinship of this letter S with the aspiration is such that the Boeotians used to write H for S in certain words, saying *Muha* for *Musa*. <note>original Latin: "Sæpe vero pro aſpiratione s, ponitur in his dictionibus quas à Græcis ſumpſimus... Muha pro muſa dicẽtes."</note>

# On the Proportion of Letters

<margin>Aldus.</margin>
Whoever wishes to see and know fully the diverse nature and virtues of this letter S, he may see enough of it, expressed very elegantly, in the fourth book of the *Grammar* of Aldus <note>Aldus Manutius (1449–1515) was a celebrated Italian humanist and printer in Venice. His grammar was a standard textbook.</note>, in the third article of the chapter titled *On the Seven Modes of Common Syllables*.

<margin>Note here the beautiful ancient fashion.</margin>
This letter S, as I said just now, is called in Greek *Sigma* from *sizein* <note>original: "$\Sigma\iota\gamma\mu\alpha$ παρὰ τὸ $\sigma\acute{\iota}\zeta\epsilon\iota\nu$."</note>. That is to say, "hissing," and such a screeching sound as a hot and red iron makes when one plunges it into water. *Sigma*, then, signifies and denotes Silence, for which reason the Ancients very often wrote it all alone above the doorway of the place in which they ate and drank accompanied by their good friends. This was to place before their eyes the idea that the words and talk held at the table ought to be sober and kept in silence. Which thing cannot be done if there is an excess of too much drinking and eating, which are things irrelevant to the decorum <term>honneſteté: In this context, Tory uses this word to mean social propriety, integrity, and the moral "honesty" expected in polite company.</term> of the table and to gracious company. On this subject, Martial <note>Marcus Valerius Martialis (c. 38–104 AD), a Roman poet known for his twelve books of *Epigrams*.</note> in his ingenious *Epigrams* has said:

<margin>Martial.</margin>
> Jokes without bitterness shall be present, nor must freedom of speech be feared in the morning, and there shall be nothing said that you would wish to have kept silent. Let my guest talk of the Green and the Blue <note>original: "De Praſino... venetóque". These refer to the rival chariot-racing factions in Rome; Martial is suggesting that table talk should stay on light, sporting topics rather than dangerous politics.</note>, and let our cups make no man a defendant.

"At my banquet," he says, "there shall be joyful words without bitterness, with the freedom to speak as if one were sober <note>Tory translates the Latin "mane" (in the morning) as "à iun" (fasting or sober), implying that the conversation should be as responsible as that of a person who hasn't been drinking.</note>, with language of such a sort that you would not wish to have left unsaid. In short, let my friend at the table speak of one thing and another, in such a way that my wine does not trouble his words."

### Book Three

<margin>Virgil.</margin>
**Sigma**, therefore, was a sign and a mark for the place where one banqueted honorably, without a great outpouring of words; and this place was capable of holding only seven people, which is a number both Even and Odd <note>Tory likely refers to seven as "Even and Odd" because it is the sum of three (the first odd number) and four (the first even number), representing a cosmic harmony in Renaissance numerology.</note>. <margin>S, or SHH.</margin>
I would wish, in this regard, that the Lords who take pleasure in building Palaces and Houses, and who love Paintings and emblems, would have an **S**, or **ST**, written, painted, engraved, or carved at the doors of their halls and kitchens, to secretly and manifestly impose Silence on a crowd of Chatters who make more noise after drinking than a hundred starlings at harvest time. This would be a lesson and an opportunity for both small and great to be moderate in speech, and to abstain from saying anything that was not beautiful, good, honest, and necessary.

<margin>Mention of the People of Toulouse and Gascons.</margin>
I return to the doctrine of our **S**, and find that the people of Toulouse and the Gascons commit an abuse in pronouncing it, for they place an **E** before it, so that if they wanted to say *schola* <note>Latin for "school."</note>, or *scribere* <note>Latin for "to write."</note>, or similar words beginning with **S**, they would say *Eschola* and *Escribere*. I do not know if this said vice has come to them because we say *escripre* and *escole* in our French language, and because in some words we place **E** before **S**, in imitation of the Greeks who write and pronounce **Epsilon** before **Sigma**—that is to say, **E** before **Σ**—in the imperfect past tenses of verbs beginning with **Sigma**. # On the Proportion of Letters

*In Priscian's first book, he notes that when the letter **I** is placed before the consonant **V**, it is lengthened, but when that same **V** is removed, the **I** is shortened: as in, "cupiui" [I desired], which becomes "cupij"; or "Cupiueram" [I had desired], which becomes "cupieram." <margin>Alcman.</margin> *those who used this digamma in place of a shortened vowel, such as the poet Alcman:*
> "And winter like the dargon." <note>original: "Καὶ χεῖμα πῦτε δάργιον." Alcman was a 7th-century BC Greek lyric poet. The 'dargon' likely refers to a cold wind or a specific location.</note>
*For it is an iambic dimeter <note>A line of verse consisting of two iambic measures.</note>, and the **Ϝ** [digamma] must be pronounced in such a way that it creates a short syllable. Our own Latin authors are also found to have done this same thing, and in place of a consonant*
<margin>Horace</margin> *they accepted **V** as a short vowel. For instance, Horace pronounced "Syluæ" [woods] as a three-syllable word in the Epodes, in this verse:*
> "And snows bring down Jove, now the sea, now the woods." <note>original: "Niuesque deducunt Iouem, nunc mare, nunc syluæ." From Horace, Epode XIII. Here, the word "syluae," usually two syllables (syl-vae), is stretched to three (sy-lu-ae) to fit the poetic meter.</note>
*For it is an iambic dimeter joined to a heroic penthemimer <note>A half-line of five half-feet in dactylic hexameter.</note>, which cannot stand correctly unless "syluæ" is taken as three syllables.* That is to say, truly this letter **V**, when placed in the position of a consonant, once had in the Latin language exactly the same power and quality in every respect as the **Ϝ**, Digamma, had in the Aeolic language. <margin>Vau.</margin>
<margin>Varro.</margin>
<margin>Didymus.</margin>
<margin>Caesar.</margin>
**Vau**, according to its pronunciation, as witnessed by Varro and Didymus; they said it was named **Vau**, and in place of this **Vau**, Caesar <note>Tory refers to Emperor Claudius, who introduced three "Claudian letters," including the turned F (Ⅎ) to represent the consonantal V/W sound.</note> wanted to write and represent this figure here: **Ⅎ**. The Digamma (Ϝ) functioned similarly to a modern "W" or "V" sound.</note> This is something the Latins seem to follow in the perfect tenses of verbs in the third and fourth conjugations, in which the **I**, being placed before the consonant **V**, is lengthened in poetic meter; and when the said **V** is subtracted from it, that **I** remains short: as in saying: *Cupiui, cupij, Cupiueram, cupieram* <note>"I desired, I desired, I had desired, I had desired." From Horace, Epode XIII. Normally "sylua" is two syllables, but here the "u" is treated as a vowel to add an extra beat to the line.</note> This example is an iambic meter of two measures, joined by a heroic penthemimer <note>A poetic fragment consisting of two and a half feet of a dactylic hexameter line.</note>, which cannot be achieved unless the aforementioned word *sylua* is divided into three syllables.

# Of the proportion of letters

<margin>Mention of the ancient Latins.</margin> Before the Latins had adopted the letter **X** from the Greeks—which is nonetheless different in its form, for it resembles *chi* <note>The Greek letter Χ</note> and not *xi* <note>The Greek letter Ξ</note>—they used to write the aforementioned letters **C**, **S**, and **G**, **S** in place of the said **X**. They wrote in this manner: *Apeccs* for *apicis*, *Regs* for *regis*, *Nucs* for *nucis*, and *Gregs* for *gregis*, as I have seen in Rome on certain ancient epitaphs, and as one can still see in the *Book of Epitaphs of Ancient Rome*, recently printed in the said city of Rome, where I was then a resident.

<margin>The prefix "Ex" in compound words.</margin> When this monosyllabic preposition, **EX**, is combined with words beginning with **S**, the said **S** must neither be written nor pronounced, because three consonants cannot exist together; as when one says *Ex* and *sequor*, it becomes *Exequor*. <margin>Priscian.</margin> Priscian <note>A famous Latin grammarian from the 6th century.</note> bears witness to this in the previously cited first book and passage, when he says:

> "For neither S, nor any other consonant, can be doubled when another consonant precedes it." <note>original: "Nunquam enim S, nec alia consonans geminari potest alia antecedēte consonāte."</note>

Never, he says, can **S** or any other consonant be doubled after another consonant. Therefore, since **X** is a double consonant, it cannot tolerate an **S** following it. Many writers do not observe this rule, for lack of paying proper attention.

<margin>Writers, pay attention here.</margin> I see many men who err in the proper pronunciation of **X** in these words: *Exaro* <note>To plow up</note>, *Exerceo* <note>To exercise</note>, *Exequor* <note>To perform or follow through</note>, and in a thousand other terms written with this preposition *ex*. They say "Ex," pronouncing it as *yeuxaro*, *yeuxerceo*, *yeuxequor* <note>Tory is criticizing a contemporary French tendency to add a "y" or palatal sound to the prefix</note>, which is a great vice in the Latin language. If they wish to learn to pronounce correctly by following the rules of the good authors named above, they should speak as if it were written *Ecsaro*, *Ecserceo*, and *Ecsequor*, and they will pronounce it very well.

# On the Proportion of Letters

*The letter of Pythagoras, divided by its two-horned split,*
*Seems to present the image of human life.*
*For the steep path of virtue seeks the right-hand track,*
*And offers a difficult entrance to those first beholding it;*
*But it provides rest to the weary at the very summit.*
*The broad way displays a soft journey, but its final goal*
*Casts down those it has captured, and rolls them through sharp rocks.*
*For whoever overcomes hard trials through the love of virtue,*
*He shall prepare for himself both praise and honor,*
*But he who follows idleness and sluggish luxury,*
*While his careless mind flees from the labors set against him,*
*Vile and destitute, shall spend a wretched lifetime.*
<note>original Latin: "Littera Pytagoræ diſcrimine ſecta bicorni, / Humanæ vitæ ſpeciem præferre videtur. / Nam via virtutis dextrum petit ardua callem, / Difficilemque aditum primum ſpectantibus offert: / Sed requiem præbet feſſis in vertice ſummo. / Molle oſtentat iter via lata, ſed vltima meta / Præcipitat captos, voluitque per ardua ſaxa. / Quiſquis enim duros caſus virtutis amore / Vicerit, ille ſibi laudemque decuſque parabit, / At qui deſidiam, luxumque ſequetur inertem, / Dum fugit oppoſitos incauta mente labores, / Turpis, inopsque ſimul miſerabile tranſiget æuum." This poem was widely used in the Renaissance to teach the "Pythagorean Y" as a symbol of moral choice.</note>

That is to say: the letter of Pythagoras <note>The Greek letter Upsilon (Y), often called the "Pythagorean letter" because its shape resembles a fork in the road.</note>, which is divided into two horns, shows us in a figure the shape of our human life, given that the noble path of virtue tends toward the right side, such that in the beginning it is narrow and very difficult, but at the end, and at the top, it widens and grants a space for rest. The other path, which is wide, presents a very easy road, but at the end and in the conclusion, there are stumbles over various horned stones <note>Jagged or pointed rocks.</note>, large pebbles, and sharp rocks. Certainly, whoever endures heat and cold and similar things to attain virtue, he shall acquire all praise and all honor. But he who, like an ignorant person, follows all idleness and all extravagance <note>original French: "bobance," meaning ostentatious luxury or pomp.</note>, while without thinking he flees from enduring work and labor, he is completely stunned that he remains infamous, poor, and wretched, and that he has miserably passed and poorly employed his time.

<margin>Young children, listen well here.</margin>
Take good care then, oh you young children, in this place, and do not leave behind the knowledge

# Of the proportion of letters

Here is the beautiful design of our last letter Zeta, which clearly demonstrates the harmony—according to both Arithmetic and Geometry—between the aforementioned seven Liberal Arts and the nine Muses with their leader Apollo. I have written at length about all of these previously in the second book, when I spoke of Virgil's pipe <note>original: "Flageol de Vergille"</note> and the Homeric golden chain. I wish to state further here that this letter Zeta is so well-constructed that in its thick stroke, which is diagonal <note>original: "de bies"</note> and extends at an oblique angle, there is such a fine arrangement in rising from the first bottom angle to the last top angle, that one finds—rendered in <margin>Nine steps.</margin> good foreshortened perspective—nine ladder rungs and steps. I have marked these according to the alignment of the small squares and shapes contained within the large square in which the said letter is constructed. Observe them well and take note of how they diminish point by point until they reach the cropped elbow <note>The "elbow" refers to the sharp bend or joint of the letterform.</note> located at the final top angle of the large square.

<margin>Moral meaning.</margin> In a moral sense, these steps and degrees signify to us the path and the ascent to blessedness <term>beatitude: a state of supreme happiness or divine favor</term>, which those who possess knowledge and perfection in "good letters" <note>This refers to the "Belles Lettres" or classical humanistic education.</note>, the Arts, and the sciences can easily attain. Regarding this, I have designed above the letter a small divine spirit standing ready to give either the Crown, the Scepter, the Palm, or the Laurel Wreath to all those who well and diligently strive to acquire knowledge, by climbing step by step until reaching its perfection, wherein lies all accomplishment of excellent prize and glorious honor.

# Of the proportion of letters

->S iij<-

I could honorably conclude my work here, but because I see many writers of Attic letters <term>Attic letters: a term used during the Renaissance to refer to classical Roman capital letters</term> who do not know how to properly create the points and distinctions <note>original: "diftinctions," referring to punctuation marks that distinguish parts of a sentence</note> that are necessary for them, according to the various meanings that arise while writing, I will provide a small design of the most necessary ones. I shall describe them briefly, just as the good ancient fathers used them in times past.

The points most required among Attic letters are the Triangular point, the Hooked point, and the Square point. The triangular point is intended to be designed and made from two turns of the compass and a straight line joined beneath those two turns of the compass. The hooked point will be well-made with two turns of the compass also, with a line crossing diagonally <note>original: "en bies"</note>, almost through the third part of the larger turn, and adhering to the smaller turn of the compass. The square point is precisely made of four turns of the compass set equidistantly, making the two at the top a little smaller than those below, as you can see in the figure that follows.

<margin>*Note here the place to position the points.*</margin>
Carefully note the placement of each point between the two outer lines of the square, for some must be set higher than others. The square point must be set exactly upon the outermost bottom line, upon which all Attic letters must be set so as to be written and proceed one after another in a balanced line. The hooked point must be set one line higher than the square point, that is to say, upon the second—

A beautiful conclusion and most notable reason.

All of these, numbering eleven, secretly and divinely testify on my behalf that I have, with good reason, divided my square for creating Attic letters <term>Attic letters: Roman capital letters inspired by classical inscriptions</term> into eleven points <note>In this context, "points" refers to the eleven parallel lines required to create the ten equal spaces, or "bodies," of his letter-designing grid.</note>, which is a manifest sign that I have not erred, but have surely and studiously understood the secret of even and odd numbers <note>original: "nombre per, & imper." Tory is referencing Pythagorean numerology, where even and odd numbers were believed to hold mystical and structural significance.</note>. That is to say, eleven points encompassing between them, at equal distances, the ten required bodies, according to the divine and yet, until now, almost unknown opinion of the noble ancients. I can truly say and conclude, without boasting, that I have drawn this ancient secret out of the shadows, and have been the first of all modern authors to bring it into clear view and into writing, to perform a devoted and heartfelt service for the public good, to which I have always dedicated myself with all my small power, and continue to dedicate myself with a good heart, bringing an end to my work, and praising our Lord God for having inspired and helped me, so much so that I have reached the perfection of the proper proportion of our good Attic letters, and to their very point.

# Declaration of Hebrew Letters.

It could have been enough, O devout lovers of good letters, that I had written to you and provided by rule the proper and true proportion of Attic letters <term>Attic letters: Tory's term for the classical Roman capital letters</term>, and had created and designed them for you by the number and measure of points, lines, and turns of the compass. But seeing that I might once again do you some honest and humble service, I thought it would be expedient and useful to presently add to the end of our total work on the aforementioned Attic letters several kinds of other good and beautiful letters. I have made them for you only without designing them by number of lines or points, like the aforementioned Attic ones, thinking that if it pleases you to follow my teaching method <note>original: "traditiue." Tory refers to the systematic principles of geometry and proportion he established in the previous books.</note> that I gave you earlier in writing at great length, at the very least by considering well the difference that may exist between one and the other, you will be able to set and create them by a certain rule and assured measure. I provide you here with various types and styles, so that you may use either one or the other at your good and virtuous pleasure.

->### of the Hebrew letters.<-

...different in form, they are used to be placed at the beginning and in the middle of words, without being allowed to be placed at the end in any way. <note>Tory is referring to the standard forms of Hebrew letters compared to their "final" forms (sophit), which were introduced on the preceding page.</note>

<margin>Pronunciation of the Hebrew letters.</margin>
Of these aforementioned twenty-seven letters, there are four that are meant to be uttered by the lips, and these are Beth, Vav, Mem, and Pe. <note>These are known as labials.</note> There are five that are meant to be pronounced with the teeth: and these are Zain, Samekh, Tsadi, Resh, and Sin. <note>These are known as sibilants and dentals.</note> There are five others that require one to pronounce them with the tongue: and these are Daleth, Teth, Lamed, Nun, and Tav. <note>These are linguals.</note> Furthermore, there are four that must be pronounced from the palate: and these are Gimel, Yod, Kaph, and Koph. <note>These are palatals.</note> There are also four others that require one to pronounce them from the throat: and these are Aleph, He, Heth, and Ayin. <note>These are gutturals.</note>

<margin>Four letters nearly similar to four others.</margin>
Note further that among the aforementioned twenty-seven letters, there are four that are similar in form to four others, and for this reason you must take great care not to be misled or deceived by their resemblance.

Therefore, these four are Beth, Gimel, Vav, and Mem, which resemble Kaph, Nun, Resh, and Samekh. <note>Tory is pointing out visual similarities that often confuse students: ב (Beth) vs. כ (Kaph); ג (Gimel) vs. נ (Nun); ו (Vav) vs. ר (Resh); and the final ם (Mem) vs. ס (Samekh).</note> Even though these are somewhat different in name and pronunciation, they nevertheless possess this difference in their said form: for the first four decline and tend toward a squared shape <term>quadrangle|A four-sided, boxy shape</term> or half-square, and the other four decline toward a circular or half-circular shape.

<margin>Names of the points serving as vowels.</margin>
The names of the points mentioned earlier, which serve as vowels <note>Hebrew is traditionally written with only consonants; vowel sounds are indicated by a system of dots and dashes called "niqqud" or points.</note>, are as follows: Pathach, Qamets, Hatef-pathach, Tsere, Segol, Shva <note>original: "Seba."</note>, Hatef-segol, Hireq, Holam, Hatef-qamets...

<margin>Method of forming syllables from letters and points</margin>
And because syllables are formed from the aforementioned letters and the aforementioned points, which serve as five vowels, you should note the manner of joining these letters. This will be demonstrated using the letter <term>Beth</term> <note>The second letter of the Hebrew alphabet, equivalent to 'B'.</note> as an example, providing a discourse through all the signs and points that serve as vowels.

Therefore, a <term>Beth</term> having beneath it the point named <term>Patach</term> <note>A short horizontal line representing an 'a' sound.</note> is equivalent to this syllable: **Ba**. And also when it has <term>Qamets</term> <note>original: "Cames". A T-shaped mark representing a long 'a'.</note> beneath it, it likewise signifies **Ba**. When it has <term>Hateph Pathach</term> beneath it, it still sounds like **Ba**. When it has <term>Tsere</term> <note>original: "Cere". Two horizontal dots representing an 'e' sound.</note> beneath it, it is equivalent to **Be**. It is exactly the same for <term>Segol</term> <note>original: "Cegol". Three dots in a triangle.</note>, for <term>Sheva</term> <note>original: "Seba". Two vertical dots representing a very short 'e' or a stop.</note>, and for <term>Hateph Segol</term>, when they are written beneath the said <term>Beth</term>. This <term>Beth</term>, having one of these beneath it, sounds and signifies **Be**. When it has <term>Hiriq</term> <note>original: "Hiric". A single dot below the letter.</note> beneath it, it signifies **Bi**. When it has <term>Holam</term> <note>original: "Holem". A dot placed above the letter.</note> or <term>Hateph Qamets</term> <note>original: "Hateph camez".</note> beneath it, it is pronounced **Bo**. <margin>Understand this well.</margin> And when it has the first <term>Shuruq</term> <note>original: "Surec". Here referring to the three diagonal dots.</note> beneath it, or the second <term>Shuruq</term> <note>The letter Vav with a dot in its middle.</note> after it, it signifies **Bu**. The sequence will thus be: **Ba, Ba, Ba, Be, Be, Be, Be, Bi, Bo, Bo, Bu,** and **Bu**. In this way, you can apply and say the aforementioned points with all the other letters, except when <term>Dagesh</term>, <term>Rafe</term>, and <term>Maphiq</term> <note>original: "Mapich". # Declaration

[People] write and place an **I** for the number one. They put two, **II**, for two; three, **III**, for three; four, **IIII**, for four. And the **V**, which is the fifth vowel <note>The author refers to the Roman numeral 'V' as a "vocal" or vowel, likely reflecting a Renaissance classification of certain letters or simply noting its position.</note>, for five. Some write and set down the numbers five hundred, six hundred, seven hundred, eight hundred, and nine hundred by using the five final letters <note>Known as *Sofit* letters, these are special forms of Hebrew letters used only at the end of a word.</note>. For common usage is to assemble the letters of the alphabet with one another in this fashion: for five hundred, they put <term>Tau</term> and <term>Coph</term> together, because <term>Tau</term> alone is worth four hundred and <term>Coph</term> one hundred. One must do the same for the other letters, adding them to one another according to the number you wish to make or write.

# Explanation of the Greek Letter.

The Greeks do not read to the Left or backwards like the Hebrews: but to the right, proceeding from the left-hand side toward the right hand. Just as the Latins and the French do.

<margin>Names of Greek letters</margin>
In the Greek language there are 24 Letters, the names of which follow: *Alpha, Vita, Gamma, Delta, Epsilon, Zita, Ita, Thita, Iota, Cappa, Lambda, Mi, Ni, Xi, Omicron, Pi, Rho, Sigma, Taf, Ypsilon, Phi, Chi, Psi,* and *Omega.* <note>The author uses spellings like 'Vita' and 'Ita' reflecting the Byzantine pronunciation common in the Renaissance, rather than the 'Beta' and 'Eta' used in modern reconstructions of Ancient Greek.</note> The Figures of the aforementioned 24 letters are as follows in Majuscules: A, B, Γ, Δ, E, Z, H, Θ, I, K, Λ, M, N, Ξ, O, Π, P, Σ, T, Y, Φ, X, Ψ, Ω. <margin>Comparison</margin>
The value and explanation of these are as follows. *Alpha* is worth as much as an **A**; *Vita* is worth a **B**, and sometimes a **V** consonant; *Gamma* is worth a Greek **G**; *Delta* a **D**; *Epsilon* is an **E**, which is to be pronounced softly; *Zita* is an **Esd** <note>This likely refers to the "ds" or "sd" sound traditionally attributed to the letter Zeta in early linguistic treatises.</note>, which is to say, such a letter as follows: Z; *Ita* is worth an **I**, long in metric syllable quantity, and is often moved and changed from Greek into Latin for an **E**, long in metric syllable quantity. *Thita* is worth a **Th**. *Iota* is an **I**, always a vowel in Greek. In Latin and in French the letter **I** is sometimes a consonant <note>The letter 'J' was often represented by 'I' during this period.</note>. *Cappa* is worth a **K**, sometimes a **C**, and sometimes this letter **Q**. *Lambda* is worth the letter **L**; *Mi* is worth **M**; *Ni* is worth **N**; *Xi* is worth the letter **X**; *Omicron* is worth a short **O** in metric syllable quantity; *Pi* is worth a **P**; *Rho* is worth **R**; *Sigma* is worth **S**; *Taf* is worth **T**; *Ypsilon* is worth a soft and mellow **I** to pronounce. # On the Greek Letter

There are four improper ones, and they are called "improper" because they are not written with each of the two full vowels standing apart: instead, the last vowel in them is somewhat diminished in its form, or changed in position. These aforementioned improper diphthongs are four in number, and are formed as follows.

<margin>
Four improper diphthongs.
ΑΙ. ᾳ.
ΗΙ. ῃ.
</margin>
The first is made of a full *Alpha*, and of a *Iota* half as small in height as the said *Alpha*. In running letters <note>The author refers to "lettre courant," which we now call minuscule or cursive script, as opposed to the formal capital letters (majuscules) used in inscriptions.</note> it is made of the said full *Alpha* and of a *Iota* converted into a very small point, placed right in the middle underneath the said *Alpha*, in this fashion: **Αι, ᾳ.** This diphthong thus formed is pronounced like **A**. <note>This "small point" is what modern grammarians call the "iota subscript." By the time this was written, the iota was no longer pronounced, hence the instruction to say it like a plain 'A'.</note>

The second improper diphthong is made in capital letters from *Ita* and from a subsequent *Iota* half as small in height as the *Ita*. In running letters, the *Iota* converted into a small point is placed directly under the middle of the said *Ita*, in this fashion: **Ηι, ῃ.** This diphthong, written thus, is intended to be pronounced like a long **I** <note>original: "I, long en quantité de ſyllabe metrique"</note> in terms of metric syllable quantity.

<margin>
ΩΙ. ῳ.
ΥΙ. ῳ. <note>The second pair here appears to be a printer's error in the original text; based on the following paragraph, it should likely represent the diphthong formed with Ypsilon.</note>
</margin>
The third improper diphthong in capital letters is made of *Omega* and a subsequent *Iota*, half as small as the said *Omega*. And in running letters, the *Iota* converted into a small point is intended to be placed directly under <note>The original French uses "sus" (above/on), but given the context of the other letters being "soubz" (under), this is likely a typographical error for "sous."</note> the middle of the *Omega*, in the following manner: **Ωι. ῳ.** This improper diphthong is intended to be pronounced like a long **O** in terms of metric syllable quantity.

The fourth and final improper diphthong in capital letters is made of *Ypsilon*

--- Page 329 ---
<meta>This page serves as the conclusion to the alphabetic sequence discussed in the previous section. While the preceding pages focused on Greek characters, this page presents the final letters of the Roman alphabet—X, Y, and Z—as conceptualized in Geofroy Tory's 1529 masterpiece, *Champ Fleury*. This work is a foundational text in French typography, where Tory sought to harmonize letterforms with the proportions of the human body and classical geometry.</meta>

# X
<note>The letter X. In Renaissance typographic theory, the X was often viewed as a symbol of balance and the intersection of the celestial and terrestrial. In his diagrams, Tory frequently illustrated this letter using a human figure with arms and legs outstretched, similar to the "Vitruvian Man," to show how the character's geometry fits within a perfect square.</note>

# Y
<note>The letter Y. Known as the "Pythagorean letter," the Y served as a powerful moral emblem during the 16th century. The stem represents the innocence of childhood, while the fork represents the "choice" an adult must make between the difficult path of virtue and the easy path of vice. Tory’s design emphasizes the elegance of this "Greek I" (i-greque).</note>

# Z
<note>The letter Z. As the final letter of the alphabet, it marks the completion of the sequence. Though often rare in Latin and French texts of the period compared to other letters, Tory treated its design with the same mathematical rigor, ensuring its diagonal stroke achieved a perfect architectural balance.</note>

->: ⬥<-
<note>A decorative lozenge or fleuron used as a terminal mark to indicate the conclusion of the alphabetical demonstrations.</note>

**Technical Vocabulary**

*   **Typography**: The art and technique of arranging type to make written language legible and beautiful.
*   **Geofroy Tory**: A renowned French humanist, engraver, and printer (1480–1533) who revolutionized the French language and book design.
*   **Champ Fleury**: Tory's most famous book, which argued that Roman capital letters should be proportioned according to the human body.
*   **Majuscules**: Large capital letters, as opposed to "minuscules" or lowercase letters.
*   **Woodcut**: A relief printing technique where an image is carved into a block of wood.
*   **Letterforms**: The specific design and shape of individual letters.
*   **Fleuron**: A typographic ornament, often shaped like a flower or leaf, used for decoration.
*   **Punctuation**: The marks, such as periods or fleurons, used in writing to separate elements and clarify meaning.

# Declaration of the Latin Letters.

<margin>
Note well
here that

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap 'A' featuring intricate floral patterns and a small classical figure seated in the background.</image-desc>After the Greek letters come the Latin ones, which I have previously in our entire work always called and named **Attic** <note>original: "Attiques"; referring to Athens or ancient Greek style</note>, and with good reason. For the greater part of the letters commonly called **Roman** letters are in value and shape purely Greek, as you can see and understand if you are willing to pay close attention.

The Romans took from the Greeks: *Alpha* [A], *beta* <note>original: "vita"</note> [B], and *Gamma* [Γ], from which they made their letter L by turning the top to the bottom. They took *Epsilon* [E], *Zeta* [Z], the long vowel named *Eta* <note>original: "Ita"</note> [H], and from it made their **aspiration** <note>The letter H, which represents a breath or "aspiration" rather than a vocalized sound</note>. They took *Iota* [I], and *Kappa* <note>original: "Cappa"</note> [K]; they took, I say, *Lambda* [Λ], and by turning the top to the bottom, made their fifth vowel, V. They took *Mu* <note>original: "Mi"</note> [M], and *Nu* <note>original: "Ni"</note> [N], *Omicron* [O], and *Rho* [P], from which they made their letter, P. They took *Tau* <note>original: "Taf"</note> [T], *Upsilon* [Y], and *Chi* [X], from which they improperly <note>original: "abusiuemẽt"</note> made their letter X. Of all these aforementioned letters, the shapes are as follows:

A, B, Γ (thus reversed, L); E, Z, H, I, K, Λ (thus turned, V), M, N, O, P, T, Y, and X, which number sixteen in total. Therefore, of purely Latin letters, there are only C, D, G, and the letter F; yet even F is not Latin, but **Aeolian** <note>original: "Eolique"; referring to the Aeolian dialect of ancient Greece</note>, and consequently Greek: for the Aeolians who invented it are a noble nation in Greece. They made it, as I have already said several times, from a *Gamma* placed upon another *Gamma* <note>Tory is describing the "Digamma" (Ϝ), an ancient Greek letter that looks like two stacked Γ characters</note>. The letter R, in just the same way, is made from the Greek letter named *rho* [P], by adding a half-reclined leg to its belly. Thus we can conclude that the Latins have only five letters of their own: C, D, G, Q, and S.

**Technical Vocabulary**

*   **Attic**: Relating to Athens or its dialect; Tory uses it to mean "pure Greek."
*   **Roman**: The standard alphabet used in Latin and most Western European languages.
*   **Alpha, Beta, Gamma, etc.**: The names of the letters in the Greek alphabet.
*   **Aeolian**: A branch of the ancient Greeks; in typography, it refers to the "Digamma" or the ancestor of the letter F.

<summary>Geofroy Tory argues that the Latin (Roman) alphabet is almost entirely derived from Greek letterforms, demonstrating how sixteen characters were adapted through rotation or slight modification. He concludes that only a handful of letters—C, D, G, Q, and S—can be considered truly original to the Latin language.</summary>

Our French letters are not taken in this way from either the Greek or the Latin: but rather are, in their shapes, native and domestic here. The Latins, then, in both borrowed and proper letters, have twenty-three in total: A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, K, L, M, N, O, P, Q, R, S, T, V, X, Y, Z. These are, first of all, divided by grammarians into six vowels: A, E, I, O, V, Y, and seventeen consonants: B, C, D, F, G, H, K, L, M, N, P, Q, R, S, T, X, Z. The vowels are divided into two groups: into prepositive <note>original: "præpositiues"; vowels that are placed before another to form a single sound or diphthong</note> and into subjunctive <note>original: "subiunctiues"; vowels that follow another to form a diphthong</note>. The prepositives are three: A, E, O. The subjunctives are also three: E, V, I. The *ypsilon* [Y] remains without being placed before or after in a Latin diphthong, but in a French diphthong, it is very often, and in several ways, subjunctive, as you may easily recognize by reading books in the French language.

# Declaration of French Letters.

<margin>Note why they are called *Cadeaulx*.</margin>
In our common use in France, we have several manners and fashions of letters. We have *Cadeaulx* <note>original: "Cadeaulx"; large, flourished calligraphic initials used to decorate the start of sections</note> which serve to be placed at the beginning of handwritten books and at the beginning of verses also written by hand. These *Cadeaulx* should be taller than the linear letters that follow them, by a quarter of the height. And for this reason, they are called *Cadeaulx*, almost as if they were *Quadreaulx* <note>original: "Quadreaulx"; a play on "quadrer" (to square or align) and "quart" (a quarter)</note>, because they must square and align by a quarter with their linear and textual letters. The Masters of Writing <term>Descripture</term> <note>an archaic term for calligraphy</note> arrange and enrich them with foliage, faces, birds, and a thousand beautiful things at their pleasure to create their displays of skill. Sigismondo Fanti, a noble of Ferrara, in his book entitled:

<margin>Sigismondo Fanti.</margin>
*Thesaurus of Writers* <note>original Latin/Italian: "THESAVRO DE SCRITTORI"; a famous 1514 writing manual by Sigismondo Fanti</note> has made them with good order, except that they are too meager and starved. I give them to you here following in their ordinary order, and without having slashed them. If you wish to enrich them, do so at your own good pleasure.

<margin>Blackletter.</margin>
Quite similarly, we have *Lettre de Forme* <term>Blackletter</term> <note>also known as Gothic script, the dense, angular type used in early printing</note>, which should be five times as high as it is wide in the short stem, as in the "I" and other stems that are made from the said "I". Long letters, such as b, d, f, h, k, l, p, q, s, t, x, z, should be seven times as high as they are wide. This is something the aforementioned Sigismondo Fanti did not observe well enough in his book, for he made them too long and meager.

<margin>Bastard Script.</margin>
Beyond Blackletter <note>original: "Lettre de Forme"</note>, we have Bastard Script <note>original: "Lettre Bastarde"; a more fluid, slanted style of Gothic script common in France</note>, which is created with nearly the same skill as the aforementioned Blackletter, except that it is thinner and is meant to be written almost like a cursive hand <term>Lettre courant</term>. The aforementioned Sigismondo sought to construct it in his book using squares and circles, but he was mistaken, making it too "starved" and thin, and by splitting the tops of the long letters <note>such as the stems of 'b', 'd', or 'l'</note> into two points, as well as the tails of said long letters.

<margin>Torneure Script.</margin>
Furthermore, we have *Torneure* letters <note>original: "Lettres de Torneure"; a rounded, ornamental style of Gothic display script</note> with which the Ancients wrote epitaphs upon the tombs of the deceased. They also wrote with them on stained glass and in tapestries, as can be seen in many old monasteries; but today, printers use them for the beginnings of their books and for their chapters.

<margin>Various names for printing types.</margin>
In printing, there are many different styles of letters. Such as Blackletter, which is called *Canon* <note>a large size of type often used in church law books</note>. Bastard script, which has always been used until now to print books in French. There is Round script, Bourgeois script, *Summula* script <note>original: "Lettre de sommes"; a script used for scholastic texts like Thomas Aquinas's *Summa*</note>, Roman script, Greek script, Hebrew script, and

# Bâtarde Script

a b c d e f g
h i k l m n o

<note>original: "LETTRE BASTARDE."</note>

<note>The <term>Bâtarde Script</term> (or "Bastard" script) is a hybrid style of handwriting that became highly popular in the 14th and 15th centuries, particularly in France and Burgundy. It is called "bastard" because it is a mixture of two styles: the formal, rigid **Gothic Textura** used for Bibles, and the faster, more fluid **Cursive** used for business and legal documents. It was often used for luxury books written in the common tongue (vernacular) rather than Latin.</note>

<note>In this specimen, you can see the scribe demonstrating the lowercase letters from **a** through **o**. Key features of this hand include the pointed, tapering descenders (the "tails" of the letters) and the decorative loops on the tops of letters like **b** and **d**, which give the script its elegant, rhythmic appearance.</note>

<summary>This page presents the first half of the lowercase alphabet in the Bâtarde script, a hybrid calligraphic style used for elegant vernacular manuscripts.</summary>

<meta>Following the conclusion of the traditional Fraktur alphabet on the previous page, this document introduces a new sequence titled "Fantastic Letters." -># FANTASTIC LETTERS<-
<note>original: *Lettres Fantastiques*</note>

**F**
The letter **F** is represented by a scythe. <note>In French, *une faux*. This large agricultural tool for reaping grain is arranged so the blade forms the top horizontal bar and the handle forms the vertical stem.</note>

**G**
The letter **G** is represented by two linked metal rings or horse bits. <note>original: *des mors*. These pieces of equestrian equipment are used here to suggest the circular and interlocking form of the letter.</note>

**H**
The letter **H** is represented by a sickle. <note>original: *une faucille*. This curved harvesting tool is positioned to suggest the shape of the character.</note>

**I**
The letter **I** is represented by a knife or dagger. <note>original: *un couteau ou un poignard*. The straight, vertical nature of the blade makes it a natural substitute for this slender letter.</note>

**K**
The letter **K** is represented by a broadaxe or cleaver. <note>original: *une hachette*. The angle of the blade against the wooden handle creates the distinct "arms" of the letter K.</note>

<column-break/>

**A**
The letter **A** is represented by an open pair of compasses. <note>original: *un compas*. A symbol of the mathematical and architectural arts, the hinged legs of the compasses perfectly form the triangular apex of the letter A.</note>

**B**
The letter **B** is represented by a pair of bellows. <note>original: *un soufflet*. This tool, used to stoke fires in a hearth, provides the two rounded "bellies" required for the letter.</note>

**C**
The letter **C** is represented by a curved iron handle or bracket. <note>original: *une poignée*. The arc of the wrought iron mimics the curve of the character.</note>

**D**
The letter **D** is represented by a carpenter's square or joining tool. <note>original: *une équerre*. This tool of the building trade provides the rigid, structural frame of the letter.</note>

**E**
The letter **E** is represented by a bow and arrow. <note>original: *un arc et une flèche*. The tension of the bow and the placement of the arrow are used to represent the horizontal strokes of the letter.</note>

# BRIEF INSTRUCTIONS FOR
## MAKING MONOGRAMS

<margin>Diversity of desires.</margin>
**O**ne <note>The original French begins with an ornamental drop cap "O".</note> could also make monograms <term>Monograms: The text uses the word "Chifres," which in this period referred to interlaced initials or decorative ciphers used by the nobility.</term> from Greek letters, by linking and interlacing them with one another. One could also certainly use many other various types of letters according to how the pleasure of the Lord or the Lady, or both of them, might wish to choose. Different people desire them in different ways. I see some who arrange and make them quite well, and these are those, as I have said before, who make them from two or three whole letters. I see others who add so many letters to one another that not a single one of the said letters remains whole, and what is worse, they make some of them missing parts, others mutilated, and others half as small, which is against the art of all good lettering. You should note that
<margin>Letters are so noble and divine that they do not wish to be mutilated.</margin>
letters are so noble and divine that they do not wish to be in any way counterfeited, mutilated, or changed from their proper shape. For as I have said and testified most abundantly in
<margin>A very beautiful and good comparison.</margin>
many places throughout our work and book, they resemble the human body, upon the proportions of which I have designed for you the Attic letters <term>Attic letters: Tory's term for classical Roman capital letters, which he argued were designed according to the ideal proportions of the human form.</term>. If one were to remove the arm, the leg, or the head of a man, he would no longer be a man, but would rather resemble a stump or a truncated tree. In the same way, whoever mutilates a

<meta>This page continues the discussion by Geofroy Tory on the proper design of "chifres" (monograms). On the previous page, Tory compared letters to the human body, suggesting that just as a person without an arm is mutilated, a letter missing a stroke is no longer a true letter.</meta>

<header>Instruction</header>

<margin>
Another beautiful and good comparison.
</margin>

...a letter, in whatever way it may be <note>This sentence completes the thought from the previous page: if a letter is mutilated like a human body, it loses its essence.</note>, it is no longer a letter, but a **distortion**, or something so wretched that one could not give it a name appropriate enough, unless one wished to say it was a **monster**. On the other hand, putting and assembling too many letters together results in them not being able to be known or discerned, any more than fifteen or twenty men could be known and discerned if they were all on top of one another in a heap. When one sees two men on their feet near each other, or three, or truly four, one can easily discern one from the other; but even with the number of four, there is still someone who cannot be well seen in his entirety because of the obstruction caused by the one in front of him. And therefore, my good lords and devout lovers of good letters <note>Tory is addressing the "Humanists" of his day, who were scholars and patrons dedicated to the revival of classical learning and beautiful typography.</note>, when it pleases you to make <term>monograms</term> <note>original: "chifres"</note> in gold rings or otherwise, make them of two, three, or four letters, without corrupting or diminishing a single one from its proper shape, and you will do very well.

I have previously shown you ten ways only, some of two letters, others of three, some of four, and others of more; but I made those of more not to induce or persuade you that you should always do so, but to show you that too great a multitude of letters placed one upon the other become confounded among themselves and do not have such good grace together as do two, three, or fou... <note>The text cuts off mid-word as the page ends.</note>
